en: *The Sutra of Old Miscellaneous Parables*, Volume One,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Kang Senghui of India during the Wu Dynasty.
(1) Once, innumerable eons ago, there was a merchant known as Sabhāhu who traveled to another country.
Selling his merchandise, he stayed near the home of a disciple of the Buddha.

At that time, the disciple’s family performed great meritorious deeds, providing high seats for the assembly of monks to preach and discuss the Dharma. They taught that good and evil arise from the mind and are manifested through the actions of body and speech, as well as the Four Noble Truths and the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.

A traveling merchant came at that time to stay and listen; his mind was awakened and he took faith and joy, whereupon he received the five precepts. He addressed the *upāsaka* elders, who exhorted and gladdened him with the Dharma, saying: "Good son!..."

For one who protects body, speech, and mind and is fully endowed with the ten wholesome actions, there are five deities for each precept; thus, the five precepts possess twenty-five deities. These manifest in the present life to provide protection and ensure that no injustice or calamity befalls them, and in future lives, they lead them spontaneously to the Great Way of Non-action.

Upon hearing the Dharma, the merchant was filled with immeasurable joy. Later, when he returned to his native country, he found that there was no Buddha-Dharma anywhere in the land. Fearing that there would be no one to receive the teachings if he were to preach them, he used the Dharma he had received to instruct his parents, brothers, wife, children, and all those both near and far; they all then came to revere the Dharma.

A thousand *li* from the land of the merchants lies a kingdom whose people are abundant, joyful, and rich in fine treasures. For more than a hundred years, these two countries have been blocked and cut off, with no further communication between them. This is because *yakṣas* dwell along the road; whenever they catch a person, they devour them, having done so countless times before and after. For this reason, the route has been severed, and no one travels back and forth.
The merchant thought to himself:

"I have observed the Buddha's precepts exactly as taught in the sutras, and there is no doubt that the twenty-five deities will provide their assistance. Even if those ghosts allow only one person to pass, I shall go and subdue them; I will certainly succeed."
At that time, there were more than five hundred fellow merchants who said to the crowd:
"I possess extraordinary powers capable of subduing ghosts; if you all can go to him, you will obtain great benefit."
The people deliberated among themselves:
"The two countries have not communicated for a very long time; if we can reach them, the gain would be beyond measure. They then agreed with one another, set out upon the road, and departed.
On the way, he came upon a place where ghosts fed; human skeletons, bones, and hair lay scattered in disarray across the ground. The Sārthavāha thought to himself:
"The evidence of what these spirits have devoured before and after is now manifest. Death is my own due lot, but I fear for these people."
He then addressed the group: "Stay here;
I wish to advance alone. If I overcome the demon, I shall return to welcome you; if I do not return, know that I have met with harm, and each of you should retreat and no longer advance."
Thereupon, he proceeded alone; after traveling several li, he encountered a ghost approaching. He maintained a correct mind, recited the Buddha's name, and remained steadfast and fearless.
When the ghost arrived, it asked: "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am a guide who has attained the Way.
The ghost laughed loudly and said:
"Do you hear my name? And yet you wish to open the way?
said the Sārthavāha.

"I know you are here, which is why I have come to seek you out. I shall fight with you; if you are victorious, you may eat me, but if I am victorious, I shall open the way for the myriad people and increase the benefit of the world."
The ghost asked,
"Who should strike first?
The merchant replied:
"I have come to seek you out; therefore, you ought to descend first.
The ghost agreed to this.

He struck it with his right hand, but the hand entered the ghost's belly and could not be withdrawn because it was so firm. He struck again with his left hand, which also entered; likewise, both feet and his head all entered the ghost, so that he could no longer move.
Thereupon, the yakṣa questioned him with a verse:
"Though your hands, feet, and head—these five parts—are bound and fettered, you should simply face death; why do you leap and bound about?"
“Though my hands, feet, and head—these five limbs—are bound, I shall hold my mind like a diamond and never let you tear it apart.
I am the king among spirits; though I have become a ghost, I possess great strength.”
"In the past and present, I have devoured creatures like you; their number cannot be reckoned.
Now that your death is near, why do you speak such delusory words?
This body is impermanent; I long ago desired to cast it aside."
Now Māra has fulfilled my wish; I shall take these and bestow them as a gift.
By this cause, I shall attain perfect enlightenment and realize unsurpassed wisdom.
My resolve is that of a sublime Mahāsattva, rare indeed within the three realms.
"Having become a teacher who delivers others, you shall soon be fully prepared to lead as a general.
I pray that you accept me as your follower; I prostrate myself with my head at your feet.
Thereupon, the yakṣa accepted the five precepts, cultivated a heart of compassion for all sentient beings, paid his respects, and withdrew into the deep mountains.

The Sārthavāha called out to the multitude once more and proceeded toward that land; thus both nations came to know that the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Deeds could subdue demons and open the Way, and they recognized that the Buddha-Dharma is most true and immeasurable. All together they upheld the precepts, honored the Triple Gem, and brought peace to their kingdoms.
That he later ascended to heaven and attained the Way was due to the power of the merit of the virtuous and faithful Upāsaka who observed the five precepts.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The caravan leader at that time was none other than myself."
"When a Bodhisattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), his deliverance is like this.

(2) Innumerable kalpas ago, there was a peacock king who, accompanied by five hundred female peacocks, traveled through various mountains. He saw a blue peacock of exquisite color and beauty; he then abandoned his five hundred wives to pursue the blue peacock. That blue peacock fed only upon nectar and excellent fruits.
At that time, the King’s consort fell ill and dreamed of the Peacock King during the night. Upon waking, she informed the King:
"Your Majesty should offer a generous reward to seek him out.
The King then commanded his master archer:
"Whoever can bring the King of Peacocks here shall be granted a hundred *jin* of gold;
I shall give my daughter as a wife to him.
The archers then distributed themselves across the mountains, and upon seeing the peacock following a blue jay, they smeared trees everywhere with honeyed flour.

Every day the peacock would take food for the blue jay; through such habitual familiarity, a man smeared his own body with honeyed flour, and the peacock immediately took the honeyed flour, whereby the man captured it.
He said to the man:
"I will give you gold from a mountain; you may release me.
The man said:
"The King has already given me gold and a wife; this is sufficient for my needs.
He then took this matter and reported it to the Great King.
The Peacock said to the Great King:

"Because the King holds his consort in such high esteem, we have come to fetch water for you. We pray that you will grant us this water so that we may recite mantras over it; let her drink it and bathe in it. If she does not recover, it will not be too late for us to kill you."
The king then gave him water over which he had recited mantras and presented it for the queen to drink; her illness was thereby cured.
All the various hundredfold ailments within and without the palace were entirely healed by means of this water, and those among the king’s subjects who came to fetch the water were beyond counting.
The peacock said to the Great King:
"It would be better for my feet to be bound with wood so that I may move freely in and out of the lake while chanting mantras, allowing the people near and far to take water as they please."
The king said, "Excellent.

He then led the wood into the lake waters and personally applied the utmost ritual control and incantations. When the people drank the water, those who were deaf or blind regained their sight and hearing, and those who were lame or hunchbacked were all restored to full extension.
The peacock said to the Great King:
"All the various evil diseases within the kingdom have been completely cured. The people honor me no differently than they would a celestial deity; I have no intention of ever leaving."
"Great King, you may release my feet so that I may fly back and forth, entering and exiting the waters of the lake, and stay to sleep upon this beam tonight.
The king then ordered them to release him; thus, for several months, he laughed loudly upon the beam.
The king asked, "Why do you laugh? He replied:
"I laugh at the three kinds of folly in the world:
first, the folly of myself; second, the folly of the hunter; and third, the folly of the king.
Accompanied by five hundred women, I abandoned my pursuit of a blue jay and was caught by a hunter through my greedy desire—this is the folly of myself."
"The hunter who refused a mountain of gold, saying that the King would give him his wife along with the gold—that hunter is a fool.

The King has obtained a divine physician; yet the King, having acquired this divine physician, does not hold him firmly but instead releases him—this is the King’s folly. All those among the King’s consorts, the crown prince, and the people of the realm who were ill have been completely cured and have become even more handsome."
The peacock then flew away.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"At that time, the peacock king was I myself; the king at that time was you; the queen at that time is now the wife of Devadatta; and the hunter at that time was Devadatta."
(3) Once there was a king who, while out hunting in a vast marshland, became extremely hungry, thirsty, and exhausted. Seeing from afar a cluster of trees and a house, he immediately went toward it.
Among them was a woman; when the king requested food, drink, fruits, and such things from her, she provided everything he sought.
The king invited the woman to meet him, but his attendant reported:
"She is naked and wears no clothes."
The king immediately took off his garment and gave it to her, but a natural fire spontaneously burned the garment; this happened three times in succession.
Startled, the king asked the girl, "What is the cause of this?"
The woman replied, “In a previous life, I was the wife of a king. When the king provided meals for śramaṇas and brahmins and wished to offer them garments as well, I said at that time:
‘It will suffice to provide the meals; there is no need to give garments.’”
"Therefore, she undergoes this retribution.

If Your Majesty would think of her and provide robes for the śramaṇas and practitioners within the kingdom—specifically those who are versed in the Buddhist scriptures—they may offer prayers on behalf of the woman so that she may be liberated from this toil and suffering."
The king accepted his words and returned to his kingdom to have robes made, yet he was unable to find a śramaṇa who had attained the Way.
At that time, there was no one in the kingdom who understood the Buddhist scriptures; the king recalled this and asked Śāradvatīputra’s father if he might know.
Dudu said: "In the past, there was a man who had no money; he simply gave me one scroll of the *Pañcaśīla Sūtra* for me to read.
The King said:
"If you know the Buddha's sutras, then give me this robe.
He then led his father to offer a blessing, saying:
"May this naked woman obtain immeasurable merit and be liberated from her arduous suffering."
The woman was wearing new clothes at the time of her death; therefore, though she had been in the realm of hungry ghosts, she shall now be reborn in the First Heaven.
(4) Long ago, by the seashore, there was a king who went out hunting and captured a śramaṇa. He made the śramaṇa his servant, and one night the śramaṇa recited a sūtra with a Brahma-like voice.
The king said, "This is a master of the arts of song; whenever there is a guest, he always performs this art."
At that time, there was a merchant who was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) from another country who traveled to that land. The king invited him and ordered the śramaṇas to sing.

Upon hearing the exposition of the profound sūtras, the lay follower’s heart leaped with joy, and he departed immediately. The people of the country went to ransom him by the tens of millions; when they reached thirty million, the king finally released him.
The merchant paid his respects and said, "I have ransomed you for thirty million, wherever you may go."
The practitioner of the Way immediately snapped his fingers and leaped into the air, saying:
"You may redeem yourself, but you cannot redeem me. Why is this?"
In the past, when I was a seller of onions, you came to me to buy some; before you had paid the three coins, I granted you my leave, yet you did not return the three coins.
"Now that you have fathered offspring, even up to thirty million, you must repay the original three coins.
The master then understood, repented his transgression, received the five precepts, and became an upāsaka.
The Master said:
"A debt, whether large or small, must not be shirked, nor can it be borne by another.

(5) When the Buddha was in the world, there was a young boy living with his elder brother’s wife. The boy went to the Buddha every day to receive the sutras and precepts, and although his brother’s wife tried to dissuade him, he would not stop.
Later, he seized the boy, pulled him close, and beat him with a staff, saying, "The Buddha and the Sangha of bhikṣus shall save you!

The boy cried out in terror and took refuge in the Triple Gem; immediately, he attained the stage of Srotāpanna. Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, the boy was able to fly away together with his wooden bonds, passing through walls and entering walls, traversing the earth and entering the earth, acting with complete mastery.

When the elder brother and his wife saw this, they were struck with terror and prostrated themselves, repenting their transgressions. The son then explained the conduct of good and evil to them, and together they went to the Buddha’s presence to receive the precepts.

The Buddha then revealed to them the origins and details of their past lives; their elder brother and sister-in-law were filled with joy, their minds were opened, their defilements were removed, and they attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
(6) Once, there was an Arhat who was practicing the Path in the mountains together with a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*). The novice went to the house of a lay follower every day to receive alms-food.

As the Master traveled along the embankment, the path was so rugged and perilous that he frequently fell down, overturning his bowl and spilling its rice into the mud and soil. The śrāmaṇera would take the uncontaminated rice and place it in the Master’s bowl, while taking the contaminated rice, washing it, and eating it himself; this continued for more than a single day.
The Master asked,
"For what reason did you discard the flavor of the rice while washing? He replied:
"When he went out for alms in the morning and returned in the rain, the rice in his bowl was overturned as he fell to the ground on the embankment.
The Master remained silent and contemplated this; realizing it was the dragon's harassment of the śrāmaṇera, he rose and went to the embankment, where he took up his staff and struck and shook it.
The dragon transformed himself into an old man and came, prostrating with his head to the ground.
The śramaṇa said,
"For what reason have you harassed my śrāmaṇera?"
He replied, "I did not dare to disturb you; I truly admired your appearance.
The dragon said:
"Why do you say that his conduct is visible?
The Master replied,
"He goes out to beg for food."
The nāga said,
"From this day forward, I pray that you will dine in my abode every day for as long as my life lasts.
The śramaṇa accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
He returned and said to the śrāmaṇera, "Go and beg for alms, but eat there; do not bring any rice back.
The śrāmaṇera ate there every day. Later, seeing that his teacher’s bowl contained two or three grains of rice, fragrant and delicious, unlike any worldly rice, he asked the upādhyāya:
"Did you eat in the heavens? The teacher remained silent and did not answer.

The śrāmaṇera then observed where his teacher had eaten and entered beneath the bed to grasp its legs. While the Upādhyāya sat in meditative concentration with a focused mind, the bed rose up along with him and flew to the seven-jeweled palace of the dragon king. There, the dragon, his wife, and all the court ladies paid homage to the śramaṇa and also paid homage to the śrāmaṇera.
The Master then became aware of this and called him out, saying:
"Rectify your mind and do not move; this is no ordinary image—why do you defile your thoughts with such intent?
After he had finished his meal, the Master immediately sent him back and spoke to him thus:
"Although he possesses palaces made of the seven treasures, women, and court ladies, he is nonetheless but an animal.
You, as a śrāmaṇera, though you have not yet attained the Way, will surely be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where you shall surpass him a hundredfold; do not harbor such defiled thoughts."
He said to the śrāmaṇera:

"This hundred-flavored rice turns into frogs as soon as it enters the mouth; because your intention was evil, you spat it out, and having turned back against yourself, you withdrew it so that the rice would not enter again."
The second [miracle] was that a woman of peerless beauty wished to perform the rites of marriage with him, but she transformed into two snakes entwined together.
The third was that on the dragon’s back were upward-pointing scales; as sand and gravel grew within them, the pain reached his very heart and chest.
"The dragon has these three sufferings; for what reason do you desire them?
The śrāmaṇera did not respond, but thereafter he brooded over them day and night, ceased eating, fell ill, and died.
His spirit was immediately reborn as the son of a dragon; his majestic power was fierce and formidable. When his father’s life came to an end, he was able to escape and be born among humans.
His teacher said: "A person who has not yet attained the Way must not be allowed to see this; such a sight is reserved for those who have reached the level of a king."

(7) Once there was a king who had a daughter; her parents named her Candrāvatī. She was incomparably beautiful, and whenever the king gave her garments, robes, or precious jewels, she would immediately say they were "naturally so."
When he reached the age of sixteen, the king spoke in anger:
"This was given by me; why do you say it arose spontaneously?
Later, a beggar came to solicit alms, and the king said:
"This is indeed your husband.
The woman of the moon replied,
"So be it," and he followed after her naturally.
The beggar was terrified and did not dare to take it.
The woman said, "You are always hungry when begging for alms; why do you refuse what the king gives to you and your wife?
They then departed together from the city, concealing themselves by day and proceeding at night until they reached a great kingdom.
At that time, the king had passed away and there was no crown prince. A husband and wife were sitting outside the city when passersby asked them:
"What kind of people are you, and what are your names?"
"From which country have you come? He replied,
"Spontaneously."
Thus it continued for more than ten days.

At that time, the minister sent eight Brahmins to stand at the gate of the capital city to observe the people entering and leaving in succession, [instructing them]: "Only this couple is worthy of being observed."
At that time, the ministers of the entire kingdom together welcomed him and installed him as king.
The royal couple governed the country with the True Dharma (saddharma), and the people lived in peace and security; the subordinate kings came to pay their respects.

After the King, the father of Candrāvatī, had finished eating and departed, Candrāvatī specifically detained him. Candrāvatī had constructed a mechanical fish made of the seven precious gems; by pulling one fish, one hundred and twenty fish would appear, and by pushing one fish, the door would open. She then prostrated herself before her father and said to him:
"I have now attained spontaneity."
He replied, "The conduct of such a person is indeed so; I am not equal to it.
The Master said:

Regarding the past lives of Candraprabhā and the beggar: they were husband and wife who both worked in the fields. The husband sent his wife to fetch their midday meal. From afar, he saw his wife meeting a śramaṇa by the water’s edge on the bank; the man begged for food from the woman and she gave a portion of her rice to the practitioner, whereupon the practitioner stopped eating.
At first, seeing the two men from afar, she did not think they were doing anything wrong; yet when she took up her staff and went to see them, the practitioners flew away.
The wife said, "You have your own autonomy; do not be resentful."
The man said,
"As for the two portions, I shall eat together with him.
The Master said:

"Because he harbored malicious intent, he was reborn as a son in a poor household; later, upon seeing a practitioner, he felt joy and repented his own faults, and for that reason, he shares in this merit."
8. (Eight) Once, as the Buddha was traveling with a multitude of bhikṣus, he encountered three intoxicated men. One ran away and hid in the grass;
another sat upright, slapping his cheeks and speaking recklessly of violating the precepts;
and another rose to dance, saying:
"I have not drunk the Buddha’s wine or spirits either; why then should I fear?

The Buddha said to Ānanda, "The man who fled into the grass shall, when Maitreya becomes a Buddha, attain the state of an Arhat and be delivered. The man who sat with his cheek pressed against the ground shall, after passing through the time of a thousand Buddhas, attain the state of an Arhat and be delivered under the very last Buddha. As for the man who rose and danced, he shall attain deliverance before the end of this current age."

"In the past, there was a śramaṇa who recited the sūtras day and night. A dog lay beneath his bed, listening to the sūtras with single-minded devotion, no longer thinking of food. After many years had passed in this manner, its life ended and it attained a human form, being born in the kingdom of Śrāvastī as a woman."
When she grew up, she saw the śramaṇa Pūrṇa and ran to him, personally offering him food with joy.
Thereafter, she followed the śramaṇa and became a bhikṣuṇī; through diligent practice, she attained the state of an arhat.
9. Once, when the Buddha Vipaśyin was in the world, the various great clans of the kingdom each offered provisions at the same time to the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, there was one great clan that was poor and had nothing with which to provide for the Buddha;
they said, "We pray that if any among the assembly of bhikṣus should desire medicine, we shall provide it all."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who suffered from an illness in his body. A member of a prominent family gave him a sweet fruit to eat; having received it, the bhikṣu attained peace and was cured.
When those of great clans eventually exhaust their lifespan and are reborn in the heavens, they surpass all other devas in five respects:
first, their bodies are free from illness; second, they are handsome; third, they possess long lives; fourth, they acquire wealth and status; and fifth, they possess wisdom.
Thus, throughout ninety-one kalpas, he was reborn above as a deva and below in great noble families, never falling into the three evil realms.

Even until the time of Śākyamuni Buddha, he became the son of a family of the four castes named Prabhūtaratna; upon seeing the Buddha, he rejoiced, entered the monastic order, and through diligent practice attained the Way, being designated an Arhat.
Indeed, by bestowing even a single *yūpa* upon a high-practicing śramaṇa, one defiles an entire nation.
Long ago, there was a husband and wife who both observed the five precepts and served a śramaṇa.

There was a newly ordained bhikṣu who did not know the sūtras. When he arrived at their door to beg for alms, the husband and wife invited the practitioner to sit before them. Once the meal was finished, the couple both descended to the ground and paid homage, saying:
"We have served the practitioner since we were young, yet we have never heard the sūtras. We pray that you will open our minds and dispel our ignorance and obscurity."
The bhikṣu lowered his head and had no reply, saying:
"Alas! Alas! The husband and wife both understood each other's meaning and said:
“The world is indeed suffering.
At that moment, both attained the fruit of the path.
Seeing the two rejoice, the bhikṣu also attained the fruit of the path.
The Master said:
"In previous lives over many generations, we were three brothers who wished to study the traces of the Way; because we practiced together, we have all attained realization of the Way.
(10) Once there was a king who, returning from hunting, passed by a stupa and paid homage to a śramaṇa; his ministers all laughed at him.
The king awoke and asked his ministers:
"If there is gold in a cauldron and the cauldron is boiling, could one take it with the hand?
Is it possible? They replied:
"It cannot be obtained.
The king said,
"If you throw cold water into it, can it be obtained?"
The minister addressed the king,
saying, "It can be obtained. The king said:

"When I perform the duties of a king, my hunting and shooting are like boiling water; yet when I burn incense, light lamps, and circumambulate the stupa, it is as if cold water were being poured into that boiling water."
"Now, when one acts as a king, there are both good and evil deeds; how could there be only evil and no good?
(11) Once, there was a śramaṇa who traveled to another country; at night he was unable to enter the city and sat among the grass outside.
When night fell, a yakṣa demon came and seized him,
saying, "I shall devour you. The śramaṇa said:
"We are far apart," [the man] said. The ghost asked,
"In what way are we far apart?"
The śramaṇa said:
"You have harmed me, and I shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, while you shall enter hell; is this not a great distance between us?"
The ghost then set him down, apologized, paid his respects, and departed.
(12) Once there was a king who ordered someone to summon a friend. The friend replied to the king, apologizing:
"I have just been digging a pit in the ground, intending to bury seven treasures therein."
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly alarmed and sent someone to summon his acquaintance, who said to the king,
"I have just now dropped some jewels into a pit.
The king then again ordered his acquaintance to be summoned, and the man said to the king:
"Now we have just descended to level ground; once on level ground, we shall proceed.
The king asked, "How can you be so foolish?"
"Is he burying the seven treasures to tell people about them?
His acquaintance replied, "He intends to prepare a sumptuous and delicious meal to feed the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; that is why he is digging a pit in the ground."
Serving gruel and rice is like being cast into a pit of inferior jewels;
sweeping the ground and pouring cleansing water for the recitation of the sūtras is like being on level ground.
He said to the King:
"This treasure cannot be defiled by the five families.
The King said: "Excellent, excellent!"
"You should not have informed me sooner;
I should have informed you sooner, so that I might have repeatedly stored away treasures.

The king then opened the treasury and gave great alms, providing food for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. The Buddha then recited a pure prayer of aspiration for him, and he immediately resolved his mind upon the Way.
13 (13) In the past, members of the four castes invited the Buddha for a meal.

At that time, there was a man selling cow’s milk who was detained by a member of the great caste to eat; he was instructed to observe the fast and refrain from listening to the sutras, and only then did the guest depart.
The wife said,
"I have been waiting for you since morning before eating.
She then forcibly compelled her husband to eat, thereby destroying his intention to observe the fast.
"Even so, he will be reborn seven times in the heavens and seven times in the human world.
The Master said:
"Observing a single day of fasting provides provisions for six hundred thousand years, and furthermore, it brings five blessings:"

First, having little illness; second, physical well-being and tranquility; third, little lustful intent; fourth, little sleep; and fifth, being born in the heavens and constantly knowing one's past lives and deeds.
14 (14) The Buddha and the community of monks were invited for a meal. A certain śramaṇa and a śrāmaṇera followed behind.

On the road, they encountered a courtesan who pulled at the śramaṇa; the śramaṇa engaged in lustful desire with her, and when the act was finished, they arrived at the house where the meal was being held.
The Buddha called to the śrāmaṇera:
"Go to the foot of Mount Sumeru and fetch some sweet spring water.
The śrāmaṇera, having already attained the Way, immediately took his bowl before him and followed with palms joined; in a short while, he returned having obtained the water.
The teacher felt ashamed and abashed; repenting his error and reproaching himself, he immediately attained arhatship.
This woman was his karmic counterpart from a past life; having encountered her and exhausted his retribution, he was finally able to attain the Way.
In the past, King Aśoka daily provided food for a thousand arhats. Later, a young śramaṇa arrived and entered the palace together with those thousand practitioners.
Once the young śramaṇa was seated, he looked up and down at the king’s palace, and continued to gaze at the principal queen without ceasing.
The king harbored a sense of resentment; after they had finished their meal and departed individually, he retained the three senior monks and asked:
"From where have these youths come?
What are their names?"
"Under whom does he serve as a disciple?
He is no śramaṇa; for what reason has he entered the palace?
As she divined his physiognomy, the eyes of the Chief Queen did not blink, and she ceased her speech.

He replied: "This śramaṇa has come from India; his teacher’s name is某甲 (Mouyi), his clan name is某甲 (Mou), and his personal name is某甲 (Mou). He has come because he possesses wisdom and clearly understands the sūtras, so as to observe the seating arrangements and palaces, and furthermore, to ascend and observe the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, seeing it as exactly equal [to this world] without any difference in thought."
In a previous life, the king placed a handful of sand in the Buddha’s alms bowl, and its merit was already so vast; now, by daily feeding a thousand arhats, his blessings will be immeasurable.
As for the one whom the Lord looked upon so intently, she was the most incomparably beautiful among the sixteen thousand women; yet seven days hence, her life will end and she shall enter hell.
"The world is impermanent; it is for this reason that I regard it thus.
The king, filled with terror, called out to his consort:
"I take refuge in the Three Holy Ones!"
The practitioner said:

"Although Your Majesty provides us with daily meals for a thousand people, these thousand people cannot release the lady from her intent. Therefore, you must obtain a young śramaṇa to preach the sūtra for her; only then can she quickly perceive the Way of the Truth."

The king sent a messenger to invite the practitioner; when the practitioner returned, the king and his consort both prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground, saying, "We take refuge in you, so that our grave offenses may be lightened."

The practitioner then explained to the lady the events she had witnessed in her past lives and revealed the essentials of the Dharma; immediately, she was filled with joy, the hairs on her body stood on end, and she attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

The lady had originally been his elder sister for five hundred lifetimes as practitioners of the Way; they had made a vow in a former life that whoever first attained the Way should deliver the other.
The Master said:

"If one does not possess the knowledge of past lives, one will never understand; nor will one recognize or speak with another, and thus it will never enter one's mind. Each person has their own original teacher."
15 (15). Once there was a man named Elisa who possessed immeasurable wealth, yet he was stingy and greedy, unwilling to provide himself with fine food or clothing.
At that time, there lived nearby an old poor man who daily provided his guests with fish and meat to their heart's content without ceasing.
The four castes thought to themselves, "Our wealth is immeasurable, yet it does not compare to this old man.

They then killed a chicken, cooked one *sheng* of white rice, placed it upon a cart, and drove to a secluded place. Just as they were about to eat, having alighted from the cart, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, transformed himself into a dog and came there. He looked up and down at them and addressed the dog, saying:
"If you cannot hang yourself upside down in mid-air, I shall not grant it to you.
The dog then hung itself upside down in mid-air; the deity Caturmahārājakāyika wondered, "What plot could this possibly be?"
He said,
"If you let both eyes fall to the ground, I shall give them to you.
The dog then let both eyes fall to the ground, and the four-caste man immediately departed empty-handed.

The Heavenly Lord transformed himself into the bodies and speech of the four castes and returned riding in a carriage; he commanded his attendants to drive away and beat anyone who falsely claimed to belong to the four castes.
When the members of the four castes returned late, the gatekeepers reviled them and ordered them to leave.
The Heavenly Lord took all his wealth and gave it away in great charity; even the four castes could not return with it. When his wealth was exhausted, he went mad for its sake.
The Heavenly Lord transformed himself into a man and asked, "Why are you so sorrowful?"
He replied, "My wealth and possessions are completely exhausted.
The Lord of Devas said:
"Indeed, possessing wealth brings much sorrow; the five families of death will arrive before one knows when.

To accumulate riches without consuming them or giving them away leads to rebirth as a hungry ghost who is perpetually destitute of food and clothing; even if one escapes that state and becomes human again, one will always fall among the lowly and base. You fail to perceive impermanence; being wealthy yet stingy and greedy, you do not eat—what hope can you have?"
The Heavenly Emperor preached the Four Noble Truths—suffering, emptiness, and non-self—to him; the four castes understood his meaning and rejoiced, whereupon the Heavenly Emperor departed.
Having returned home, the four castes repented their former thoughts and gave alms with all their hearts, thereby attaining the fruit of the Path.
16 (16) Once, there was a son of a prominent family who was handsome; he had a golden image of a woman made and said to his parents, "I shall marry only when I find a daughter such as this."

At that time, there was also a woman from another country who was likewise beautiful; she fashioned a golden image of a man and said to her parents, "I shall marry only when there is someone like this."
When the parents each heard this, they brought the two together from afar and joined them as husband and wife.
At that time, the king held up a mirror to look at himself and asked his ministers,
"Is there anyone in the world whose countenance is like mine?"
He replied, "Your servant has heard that in that country there is a man of incomparable handsomeness.
Thereupon, he dispatched an envoy to invite him.
The messenger arrived and informed him on behalf of the king, saying,
"The king wishes to see the worthy one.
Having prepared his carriage and departed, he thought to himself:
"The King summoned me because of my sagacity," he thought;

he then returned to retrieve the essential arts from his books, only to find his wife committing adultery with a guest. He was filled with despondency and resentment, which caused his vital energy to become constricted; his complexion grew haggard, appearing even more hideous than before.
When I saw that this man was traveling with such hardship and his countenance was so emaciated, I immediately cleared a stall in my horse stable to provide him shelter.
One night, while he was in the stable, I saw the King’s principal consort come out to have illicit relations with a groom. At that, I realized within myself:
"If even the King’s consort behaves in such a manner, what can be said of my own wife?"
When his mind was at ease and his complexion had returned to normal, he met with the king.
The king asked,
"For what reason did you remain outside for three days?"

He replied: "When I came to welcome you, I forgot something and went back on the road to retrieve it; there I saw my wife committing adultery with a guest. In my indignation, I became bitterly enraged, my countenance changed, and I remained in the stable for three days."
"Yesterday, while at the stables, I saw the Senior Lady coming; she was having an illicit affair with a groom. If the Senior Lady is like this, what can be said of others?
My suspicions have cleared, and my countenance has returned to its former state."
The king said, "If even my wife is like this, how much more so are ordinary women?

The two men then entered the mountains together, shaved their hair and beards to become śramaṇas, and reflected that one cannot engage in worldly affairs with women; through diligent and unremitting effort, they both attained the path of a pratyekabuddha.

17 (17) Once there was a woman who gave birth to a daughter of incomparable beauty. When she was three years old, the king took her to see her; he summoned a seer to examine her, asking, "Will she later become a queen?"
The practitioner said, "This woman has a husband; the King will surely favor her later.
I shall hide her away securely."
He then called the crane forward and asked,
"Where do you dwell? The crane replied to the king:
"I dwell upon a mountain peak where there is a tree that neither humans nor beasts can pass; beneath it flows a swirling torrent where no boat can travel.
The king said, "I entrust this girl to you for your care."
He then seized her and took her away, providing her with food from the king day after day.

After a long time had passed, a large log was carried away by the current; it struck against a tree that was leaning over the water, and downstream there was a man who caught hold of the tree. He fell into the swirling waters and could not escape, but as the eddy filled up, the tree rose up and came to rest, leaning against a mountain.
A man climbed a high crane tree to have intercourse with a woman, who then hid him there.
Every day the crane carried the woman up and weighed her, saying:
"Those who have already undergone the change of body are heavy; those who have not yet done so are light."
The crane realized the girl was heavy; he searched to the left and right for a man, lifted her up, and discarded her. He then went and reported the matter to the king.
The king said, "The Daoist masters are skilled at reading physiognomy."
The Master said:
"People have karmic destinies from past lives that cannot be controlled by mere effort.
When they encounter their destined counterparts, they are naturally compatible; it is the same for all animals."
18 (18) Once there was a king who was obsessed with women. His principal consort said to the crown prince:
"I am your mother, yet since my birth I have never seen the kingdom; I wish to go out once. You should petition the king on my behalf."
Thus it was repeated three times.

The Prince addressed the King, who granted his permission. The Prince himself took the reins and drove the carriage, clearing the way for the ministers on the road. He went out to welcome and pay homage to the Lady; he drew back her hand to open the curtain, allowing the people to see her.
When the Prince saw the woman in this manner, he feigned abdominal pain and returned.
The lady said, "I am truly unfortunate."
The Prince thought to himself,
"If even my mother must come to this, how much more so for others?
That night, he abandoned the kingdom and departed, entering the mountains to wander and observe.

At that time, there was a tree by the roadside with a fine spring beneath it. The Prince climbed the tree and saw a brahmin walking alone who entered the pool, bathed, and came out to eat. He performed a magical rite and produced a jar; inside the jar was a woman, and they made a home for one another in a secluded place.

The brahmin was then able to lie down; the woman again performed a magical artifice, producing a jar from her mouth, within which was a young man. She lay with him, and having finished, she swallowed the jar.
In a short while, the brahmin rose, placed his wife back inside the jar, swallowed it, fashioned a staff, and departed.
The Prince returned to the kingdom and said to the King:
"I request that you provide food for three people—myself, the practitioner, and the various ministers—and set it aside to one side."
When the brahmin arrived,
he said, "I am here alone. The Prince replied:
"The practitioner must give up his wife so that we may eat together.
The practitioner could not refuse and gave up his wife.
The Prince said to the woman:
"Let us go out and eat with some men.
Thus he spoke up to three times, and being unable to stop him, they went out and ate with some men before departing.
The King asked the Prince:
"By what means did you know this?
He replied, "When my mother wished to view the kingdom, I was driving the chariot; she extended her hand so that people might see it."
"I recall that women are capable of great lust; therefore, I feigned abdominal pain and returned.

Upon entering the mountains, I saw this ascetic concealing his wife within his belly out of illicit intent. Such is the way of women—illicit desire cannot be severed. I pray that Your Majesty will grant clemency to those in the palace so they may move about as they please."
The king then issued an edict to the women of the harem, saying, "Those who wish to go may follow their own will.
The Master said,
"One cannot trust women in this world."
19 (19) Once, there were two men who left their teacher to study the Way and traveled together to another country.
On the road, they saw the tracks of an elephant. One man said:
"This is the track of a female elephant carrying a female calf; the elephant is blind in one eye; upon the elephant's back is a woman carrying a daughter."
Another person said,
"How could you know? He replied:
"You know this by means of mental cognition.
If you do not believe me, go before him and you shall see it for yourself.
When the two men reached the elephant, everything was exactly as he had said; subsequently, both the elephant and the man were born in such a manner.
First, he thought to himself:
"I and he have both studied under the same teacher, yet I alone have not seen the essential.
Later, he returned and informed the teacher:

"The two of us traveled together, and this man saw a single elephant footprint; he distinguished its various essential features, yet I did not understand them. I pray that the Master will explain them to me once more, without partiality."
The Master then called out one person and asked,
"By what means did you come to know this? He replied:
"This is what my teacher always says.

I saw that the elephant urinated on the ground and knew it was a female; I saw that its right foot pressed deep into the earth and knew it was carrying a calf; I saw that the grass on the right side of the path did not move and knew its right eye was blind."

Seeing that the elephant had urinated where it stood, I knew it was a female; seeing that its right foot pressed the ground deeper, I knew it was carrying a female fetus. I contemplated this with subtle and refined mindfulness alone.
The Master said:
"In studying, one must contemplate with focused intent and through subtle refinement one will attain mastery.
That those who are superficial do not reach this goal is not the fault of the teacher."
20 (20) Once there was a woman who possessed great wealth in gold and silver. She engaged in sexual relations with a man, and having taken all her gold, silver, and garments, they fled together.
Upon reaching the edge of the swift current, the man said, "Bring your wealth and goods; I will ferry them across first and shall return to fetch you.
The man then ran away and did not return.
A woman living alone by the water’s edge saw a fox that had captured a hawk, set it down to seize a fish, and then, failing to catch the fish, lost the hawk as well.
The woman said to the fox:
"How can you be so utterly foolish?"
"Catch two and you do not get one.
The fox said, "My stupidity is still tolerable, but yours is even worse than mine."

21. (Twenty-one) Once, when the daughter of a dragon king went out for a stroll, she was bound and beaten by a cowherd. When the king went abroad to tour his realm, he saw the girl, immediately released her, and allowed her to depart.
The Dragon King asked the girl,
"For what reason are you weeping?
The girl replied:
"The king has unjustly beaten me.
The Dragon King said, "This king is always compassionate; why would he beat anyone so cruelly?"
The Dragon King secretly manifested as a snake and listened from beneath the bed. The King said to his consort:
"While out walking, I saw a young daughter being beaten by a cowherd; I released her and sent her away."
The Dragon King manifested as a human tomorrow and came to meet the king, saying to him:

"Your Majesty has bestowed great kindness upon me. Yesterday my daughter was beaten by someone; it was because you went to resolve this that she survived. I am a dragon king, and I am at your disposal."
The king said, "I already possess many treasures; my only wish is to understand the speech of the hundred kinds of beasts.
The Dragon King replied:
“Observe the fast for seven days; when the seven days have passed, come and speak to me, but take care not to let anyone know.
Thus the king and his consort ate together, and they saw a female moth say to the male, “Take some rice! to which the male replied, “Each of us must take our own.”
The female said,
"My womb is uncomfortable.
The King laughed, and the Queen said:
"Why did Your Majesty smile?

The king remained silent. Later, while sitting together with his consort, he saw a moth crawling along a wall; as two moths met, they fought and struggled until they both fell to the ground, whereupon the king laughed again.
The lady asked, "What is it that you laugh at?
She spoke thus up to three times. He replied:
"I will not speak to you," [the king] said. The lady replied,
"If Your Majesty does not speak with me, I shall take my own life."
The king said, "Wait;
when I have returned from my journey, I shall speak to you.
Thereupon, the king set out on his excursion.
The Dragon King transformed himself into several hundred sheep to cross the water.
Among them was a pregnant ewe who called out to a ram, saying, "Return and wait for me. The ram replied:
"I am utterly unable to deliver you. The cow said,
"If you do not deliver me, I shall kill myself."
"Do you not see that the king will die for the sake of his wife?
The ram said, "This king is a fool to die for a wife; you are dying because you think I have no ewe."
When the king heard this, he thought to himself:
"I am the king of a kingdom; am I not even equal to the intelligence of a sheep?
Having returned home, the queen said:
"If the King does not explain it for me, I shall simply take my own life.
The King said, "If you can take your own life, that would be well; however, there are many women in my palace, so I have no need for you."
The Master said, "Foolish man!
By sitting upon his wife, he seeks to bring about his own death.
(22) Once there was a kingdom where the five grains ripened in abundance, the people lived in peace, were free from illness, and enjoyed music day and night without sorrow.
The king asked his ministers:
"I have heard that there are calamities in the world;
what are they like? They replied:
"I, too, have not seen it.
The king then dispatched a minister to a neighboring country to seek its purchase.
A celestial deity then transformed into a man selling it in the marketplace; it resembled a pig and was bound with iron chains.
The minister asked,
"What is the name of this? He replied:
“Wretched mother,” he said,
“for how much money did you sell her?”
He replied, "Ten million.
The minister then looked at him and asked:
"What kind of food do you eat?
He replied,
"I eat one *sheng* of needles every day."

The minister then went from house to house seeking needles; thus, the people met two by two and three by three, seeking needles until messengers reached every district and county in a state of turmoil, leaving everyone afflicted with distress and weary of it.
The minister said to the king, "This mother of calamity has caused the people to rise in rebellion and men and women to lose their livelihoods; we wish to kill and cast her away.
The king said:

"Excellent! he said, and then outside the city, though he was pierced with spears, hacked with axes, and crushed with weights, he did not die. He piled up firewood and burned himself until his body was red as fire; he then ran out, passing through a village and burning it, passing through a marketplace and burning it, and entering the city and burning it.

Passing through the country in this manner, he eventually caused the people to be thrown into turmoil, suffering from hunger and exhaustion. Their fondness for acquisition led to the calamity they brought upon themselves.
(23) (22) Once there was a parrot that flew and settled in another mountain. Within that mountain, the various birds and beasts cherished one another with deep affection and did not harm each other.
The parrot thought to itself, "Even so, this cannot last long; I must surely return.
And so it departed.

Several months later, a great mountain caught fire and blazed on all sides. Seeing this from afar, the parrot entered the water, took up water with his wings, flew into the air, and sprinkled the water from between the feathers of his body, wishing to extinguish the great conflagration.
As he was thus coming and going,
the deity who dwelt there said: "Ho, parrot!
"Why are you so foolish?
Could a fire a thousand *li* in size ever be extinguished by the water from your two wings?
The parrot replied:

"I do not cease to exist because of my knowledge; I once dwelt as a guest in these mountains, where the hundreds of birds and beasts were all kind and virtuous, regarding one another as brothers. It was simply that I could not bear to see them [in their current state]."
The celestial deity, moved by his utmost sincerity, sent down rain that extinguished the fire.
(24) The Buddha was traveling together with the bhikṣus and took shelter within some grass.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"For what reason did you abandon the path and travel through the grass?
The Buddha said:
"There are bandits ahead, and the three brahmins behind us will surely be captured by them.

When the three arrived later, they saw a heap of gold by the roadside; they stopped there to collect it together and sent one man back to the market in the village to buy rice. Another took poison and put it into the rice to kill the other two.
"I shall obtain the gold alone.
Again, the two of them conceived this thought; as soon as they saw him coming, they killed him together, and having eaten the poisoned rice, they both died.
Thus, each of the three gave rise to evil intentions and killed one another in succession.
25 (Twenty-five): In the past, there were four castes who kept their wives hidden so that no one could see them.
One wife happened upon a maidservant who was digging an underground cave, and she entered into an illicit liaison with a silver-smith boy.
The husband later said to his wife:
"I did not act as you say; do not speak such falsehoods.
The husband then spoke:
"I shall take you to the sacred tree," he said.
The woman replied,
"Excellent."
Having observed the fast for seven days and entered the fasting chamber, the wife spoke secretly to Silver-Carver: "What should you do?
You must feign madness and, whenever you encounter someone in the marketplace, seize them and drag them along."
When the fast was concluded, he took his wife out;
the wife said, "In my life I have never seen the market; you shall take me through it.
Zuo Yin'er then picked her up, laid her on the ground, and did as he pleased. The wife then shrieked at her husband:
"Why does this man embrace me?
The husband said,
"This is merely a madman."
The husband and wife went together to the shrine and prostrated themselves, saying, "Since birth we have committed no evil; we were merely possessed by this mad spirit.
The wife was then restored to life, while the husband remained silent and ashamed; such indeed is the nature of a woman's deceit.

26 (26). Once, there was a woman traveling as a bride, accompanied by her female companions. While they were eating and drinking and enjoying themselves on an upper terrace, a mandarin orange fell to the ground.
The women looked at it together and said, "Whoever dares to go down and fetch that orange shall have food and drink prepared for her by us all."
As she was about to go down the stairs to marry off her daughter, she saw a young boy who had already taken the oranges away.
The girl said to the boy, "Give me back the oranges. The boy replied:
"When you are about to be married, come first to me; I will promise to give you back the oranges, otherwise I will not give them to you.
The girl said, "I agree."
The youth then gave her an orange; the woman took it and returned with it, and the people together prepared food and drink.
When she was sent to her husband’s place, the woman said:
"I have a solemn vow: I wish first to see the youth, and only then shall I become your wife."
The husband then released her.
As she was leaving the city, she encountered bandits, and the woman pleaded with them for mercy:
"I have a solemn vow that must be fulfilled."
The bandits released her.
Just as she was proceeding, she encountered a man-eating demon; the woman prostrated herself, entreating him to release her from his vow, and the demon let her go.
She arrived at the gate of the youth’s house and requested to sit before him. The youth did not object; he provided her with food and drink and presented her with a piece of his private gold.
The Master said:
"In this way, the husband, the thief, the ghost, and the boy—all four are skillful;
yet even so, their intentions lie in different places."
Some say that when the husband prevails, it is because he is anxious to maintain his wife;
when the thief prevails, it is because he is anxious to seize the property;
and when the ghost prevails, it is because he is anxious to seize the food and drink.
"To say 'the youth is superior' is merely a matter of modesty.
(27) [Discourse 27] Once there was a woman who would always say:
"I have lost nothing."
The son took his mother’s gold ring, threw it into the water, and went to ask where his mother’s gold ring was.
His mother said,
"I have lost nothing."

On a later day, the mother invited Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, and Mahākāśyapa for a meal. She was to obtain fish and sent someone to the market to buy some; upon returning to prepare them, she found a gold ring inside the belly.
The mother said to her son, "I have lost nothing."
The son was filled with great joy and went to where the Buddha was, asking:
"For what reason does my mother possess this merit of not dying?
The Buddha said:
"Formerly, there was a rishi dwelling in the north. During the winter, when the cold was extreme, everyone crossed over to the south of the mountain.
At that time, there was an old widow who, being poor, was unable to go; she remained alone to guard the stored goods for the multitude."
In the spring, when all the people returned, the mother gave back each of their belongings to its respective owner, and everyone was filled with joy.
The Buddha said, "The woman who was the sole mother at that time was your own mother. Because she protected the property of others in a previous life, she obtained this merit of having nothing lost."

"In the past, there was a son of a family of the four castes who built a small dwelling for Revata that was sufficient to contain himself, and he also constructed a place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). Later, when his life ended, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There he obtained a jeweled mansion four thousand *li* in circumference, where he enjoyed all manner of pleasures at will. Rejoicing, he took celestial flowers and scattered them over the roof of Revata’s house."
The deva said:
"I merely built a small mud hut, yet I have obtained this fine palace; out of gratitude for his kindness, I have come to scatter flowers.
(28) (28) Once, there were three practitioners of the Way who asked one another:
"By what cause did you attain the Way?

He replied, "In the kingdom, I observed that the grapes were in full and excellent bloom; by the hour of *bhu*, people came to pluck and gather them until they were all scattered and ruined upon the ground. Seeing this, I realized impermanence, and through this realization, I attained the Way."
One person said:

"While I was sitting by the water's edge, I saw a woman shaking her hand over a washing vessel; the bracelets on her arms struck against one another, and through the conjunction of these conditions, a sound was produced. By means of this, I attained the Way."

One person said: "I was sitting by the side of a lotus pond and saw the flowers in full bloom. At the hour of *bhu*, dozens of chariots arrived; people and horses bathed therein and took all the flowers away. Such is the impermanence of all things! This realization of mine constitutes my attainment of the Way."

29. (Twenty-nine) Formerly, there was a brahmin of great stature, talent, and learning who engaged in polemical debate. He established groundless arguments to subvert the essential truths, citing the unreal as real and employing far-fetched analogies to ensnare others; none could withstand him, and thus he became a teacher in various kingdoms.
Later, when he arrived at Śrāvastī, he walked about during the day with a fire burning;
the people of the city asked, "For what reason is this so? He replied:
"The state is dark with ignorance; that is why he lights this fire.
The king was deeply ashamed and hung a drum beneath the city gate, seeking out wise men who could refute this man.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa who entered the kingdom and asked him,
"Why is this so? He replied:
The king was ashamed of what the brahmin had done.
When a wise man beat the drum, the śramaṇa lifted his foot and stepped over it; hearing this, the king was greatly delighted and invited the śramaṇa and the brahmin to ascend the hall for a meal.
The śramaṇa said to the king:
"Excellent is this brahmin! His wisdom is clear and penetrating; he is truly a man of the Way, neither a slave nor a laborer, nor of the lineage of those who carry out the dead."
The brahmin remained silent and had no reply.

Simultaneously, musical instruments were played; the brahmin was then placed inside a dung-scoop, his tracks were swept away, and he was driven out of the country, as the news was passed along from person to person.
30 (Thirty): Once there was a śramaṇa who, having finished his meal, trimmed [his nails], adorned his face, adjusted his robes, and peered about before and behind him.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"Is this bhikṣu so unrighteous?
The Buddha said:
"It is simply because she has just come from among women that her residual feminine mannerisms have not yet entirely vanished.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu manifested the path of an arhat and entered parinirvāṇa.
(31) Formerly, outside the city of Śrāvastī, there was the wife of a householder who was an upāsikā, fully endowed with pure conduct.
The Buddha went to her door in person to beg for alms. The woman placed rice into his bowl and then paid him homage.

The Buddha said: "Planting one yields ten; planting ten yields a hundred; planting a hundred yields a thousand; thus it grows to ten thousand and then to a hundred million, until one attains the Path of Seeing the Truths."
Her husband did not believe in the Way or its Virtue; however, he listened silently from behind as the Buddha offered his benediction, saying:
"What the śramaṇa Gautama says—how exceedingly extreme it is!"
"By giving a single bowl of rice, one obtains such merit and further attains the Path of Seeing the Truths.
The Buddha asked, "From where have you come?"
He replied, "I have come from within the city.
The Buddha said:
“How high do you see the nyagrodha tree? He replied, “It is forty *li* high;
it yields tens of thousands of *hu* of fruit each year, and its seeds are as large as mustard seeds.”
He replied, "Only a small amount.
The Buddha said:
"Was it one *sheng*? He replied,
"It was merely one seed."
The Buddha said,
"What you have said is quite excessive.
Suppose one plants a single mustard seed that grows to a height of forty li and produces several hundred thousand seeds each year."
He replied, “It is indeed so. The Buddha said:
"The earth itself does not know the power of its own retribution; how much more so for one who joyfully offers a single bowl of rice to the Buddha?
That merit is beyond measure.
At these words, the husband and wife’s minds were opened and liberated, and they immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

32 (Thirty-two): Long ago, there was a śramaṇa who had already attained the stage of anāgāmin. While dyeing his robes by boiling grass on a mountain, a man who had lost his ox went searching everywhere for it.

Seeing smoke rising from the mountain, he went to investigate and found that the contents of the cauldron were entirely cow bones. His alms-bowl had transformed into a cow’s head, and his *kāṣāya* robe had transformed into cowhide. The man then tied the bones to his head and wandered through the country, where everyone saw him together.

The śrāmaṇera, seeing that the sun had already reached midday, struck the wooden gong; not seeing his teacher arrive, he entered the room and sat in contemplation. Seeing that his teacher had been humiliated by others, he went to him, prostrated with his head at the teacher's feet, and said:
"For what reason has this happened?"
He replied,
"It is the sin of a very long time ago.
The śrāmaṇera said:
"You may return for a moment to eat.
The two of them then released their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and departed together.

The novice had not yet attained the Path and still harbored unabated anger; looking back, he saw the lay devotee and the people of the country. He thought, "These people have treated my teacher in such a manner, causing the dragon to rain down sand and stones and shaking this kingdom to terrify them."
As soon as he finished this reflection, sand rained down from all four directions, and the city walls, moats, houses, and rooms were all utterly destroyed.
The Master said:
"In a previous life, my occupation was that of an ox-slaughterer; it is for this reason that I have incurred this calamity."
"For what reason have you committed this offense?
Depart; there is no need for you to follow me further.
The Master said:
"Since such are the consequences of sin and merit, one cannot but be cautious.
(33) Once there was a king who had five ministers. One minister previously invited the Buddha, but the Buddha did not accept; the minister then returned.
Because the king invited the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"This minister’s life must surely end today; who will perform meritorious deeds tomorrow?
The minister had once had a physiognomist examine him, who said:
"I shall die by the sword.

He constantly used weapons for his own protection; he himself also drew his sword and carried it. One night, when he was about to lie down, he entrusted the sword to his wife to hold. The wife fell asleep and let the sword drop, severing her husband's head. She then cried out, saying, "My lord is dead!"
The king then summoned his four chief ministers and asked:
"While you were providing guard and protection, she instigated this wicked rebellion; yet her wife accompanied her and has suddenly arrived here. Which of those stationed at the border is guilty?"
He then severed the right hands of the four ministers.
Ānanda asked the Buddha for the reason;
the Buddha said:

"In a previous life, her husband was a shepherd boy and his wife was a white ewe. His four ministers were thieves who, seeing the boy tending sheep, called out to him and raised their right fingers together, commanding him to kill the white ewe so that they, five people in all, might cook it."

The child wept piteously as the sheep was slaughtered for the thief; thus they revolve through birth and death, and because they have now met together in this life, they must exhaust the karmic retribution of their past existences.
34 (34). Once there was a family of great lineage, whose wealth was in the hundreds of millions. They were always fond of giving alms and never refused those who came seeking.
Later, they gave birth to a son who had no hands or feet; his body resembled that of a fish, and he was named Matsyakāya (Fish-Body).
After his parents passed away, he inherited the family estate; yet, while sleeping in his chamber, no one saw him.

At that time, there was a strongman who relied on the King’s kitchen for food but constantly suffered from hunger and deprivation. He alone would haul sixteen carts of firewood, selling it to support himself, yet this was often insufficient. He went to these four classes of people to seek what he lacked, saying:
"For many years I have relied on the King’s food and drink, but they have never been sufficient; I am constantly plagued by hunger."
"Having heard that the wealth of these four castes amounts to billions, I have come to beg.
The fish-bodied being invited him to meet and showed him its physical form.
The strong man withdrew and reflected to himself:
“The strength of this stone is such that it would be better for those nearby to have no hands or feet at all, so that they could not even grasp its object.
He then went to where the Buddha was and asked about his doubts:

“In this world, there may be those as noble and honored as kings who, upon death, possess neither hands nor feet, yet have accumulated such wealth; whereas I, whose physical strength is unrivaled within my own kingdom, am constantly beset by hunger and lack sufficient food. By what cause is this so?”
The Buddha said:

"In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the fish-body and this king were both eating with the Buddha. At that time, you were poor and served as his assistant. When the fish-body had finished receiving all that he was entitled to, he set out with the king and said to him:
'I have business today and cannot go together; to neglect this matter would be no different from cutting off my hands and feet.'"
The practitioner at that time was none other than this king; the one who failed to refrain from improper speech was the fish;
and the poor man who provided assistance was you yourself.
Thereupon, the wrestler’s mind was awakened; he immediately became a śramaṇa and attained the path of arhatship.
