(35) The Buddha Preaches the Sūtra for His Disciples. At that time, there was a hunter carrying a crossbow and bearing more than ten dead birds who passed by to see the Buddha.
His intent was sharp and vigorous; he wished to hear the preaching of the sūtra and desired to listen and receive it. However, the Buddha stopped him and did not preach it for him.
When the hunter had withdrawn, he said:
"If I become a Buddha, I shall certainly preach the Way universally for all people, without any contradiction.
Ānanda then asked the Buddha:
"This person has composed works on sensual desires and listens to the scriptural teachings;
why do you oppose him? The Buddha said, "This person is a great bodhisattva whose resolve is profound and firm."
In the past, when he was a king, his mind was not impartial toward his many court ladies; those who did not receive his favor conspired together to poison him to death.
The king was born into a family of hunters, and all the court ladies fell among the birds and beasts. Now their retribution is complete, and they have subsequently attained accomplishment.
"If I were to preach the sutras for them, I fear their minds would be terrified and they would fall into the stage of an Arhat;
therefore, I do not preach for them. (36) Once, in a Buddhist temple, there was a golden cauldron used to cook the five flavors to provide for the practitioners.

At that time, there was an ordinary man who entered the monastery and saw a golden cauldron; wishing to steal it, and having no other means, he falsely assumed the guise of a śramaṇa and entered among the assembly of monks.

Having heard the Elder’s discourse on the sūtras, which explains the essentials for realizing various transgressions, merits, birth and death, and the proof that the retribution of shadows and echoes cannot be escaped, his mind was awakened within;
he felt shame and remorse, and by composing his feelings and concentrating his mind, he beheld the traces of the Path.

Reflecting on the origin of this matter, he thought, "The cauldron is my teacher. He first paid homage to the cauldron, circumambulated it three times, and then recounted the entire account to the assembly of śramaṇas.
Indeed, awakening arises from various causes; those whose minds are single-minded will surely perceive the Truth.
37 (Thirty-seven). In the past, Aniruddha had already attained arhatship; among the assembly of bhikṣus, his countenance was so upright and handsome that he resembled a woman.

Once, while walking alone through the grass, a frivolous young man saw him and, taking him for a woman, was moved by depraved desires and sought to violate him. When he realized it was a man, he looked at his own form and perceived it had transformed into that of a woman. Overcome with shame and resentment, he fled into the deep mountains and did not dare return for several years.
The wife and children in that household had not known where their father was since birth; believing him dead, they wailed in inconsolable grief.
As Aniruddha went on his alms-rounds, he arrived at their home. The woman wept and told him that her husband had not returned, begging for the power of his merit so that he might be restored to life.

Aniruddha remained silent and did not respond; his heart was filled with sorrow, and he even went into the mountains seeking to meet him. That man then repented his transgressions and reproached himself, whereupon he was restored to manhood and was finally able to return home to see his family.
In general, one must not treat those who have attained the Way with ill intent, for one will instead incur their calamity.
(38) Once there was a bhikṣu who sat beneath a solitary tree in a secluded place and practiced the path with focused intention.

There was a monkey in a tree who, seeing the bhikṣu eating, descended and stayed by his side. The bhikṣu gave him some leftover rice; having received the food, the monkey immediately went to fetch water to provide for his washing.
This continued for many months.

One day, the monk suddenly forgot to set aside food for his meal and did not leave any behind. The monkey, unable to obtain food, became enraged; he took the bhikṣu’s *kāṣāya* robe, climbed a tree, and tore it to pieces.
The bhikṣu was angry with this monkey and struck it with a staff; by mistake, the blow struck the ground, and the monkey died immediately.
Several other monkeys came together in a clamorous uproar, carried the dead monkey away, and brought it to the Buddhist temple.
The community of bhikṣus, knowing that there must be a reason for this, assembled all the bhikṣus and inquired into his intention. The bhikṣu then related the facts in full.
Thereupon, an instruction was established:
"From this day forward, whenever a bhikṣu eats, he must always portion out and set aside a remainder to give to crawling creatures; he must not consume it entirely."
The practice of donors begging for alms-food originated from this incident.
(39) Once, there was a tortoise who encountered a severe drought; the lakes and marshes dried up, and he could not reach a place where food was available.
At that time, a large crane was perched nearby; the turtle appealed to it in distress, begging for deliverance. The crane pecked at him and carried him away, flying over various cities and towns.
The turtle did not remain silent, but asked, "What is this?"
When he did not stop doing so, the crane responded; as it responded, its mouth opened, and the turtle fell to the ground, where people captured it, butchered it, and ate it.
Thus, when a person is foolish and stubborn, lacking foresight, and fails to guard their speech, this is the analogy for such a case.
In the past, there was a śramaṇa who had an ordinary person shave his head. Once the shaving was complete, he prostrated with his head and face touching the ground and said:
“I pray that in future lives my mind and intentions may be pure and clean, and my wisdom may be like that of this practitioner.”
The practitioner said,
"May you attain wisdom that surpasses mine.
The man paid his respects and departed.

Later, when his life ended, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; when his lifespan there ended, he descended and was born as a son into a great clan. Subsequently, he became a śramaṇa and attained the vision of the traces of the Path through wisdom—all of which resulted from the power of his resolute intention.
40. Once there was a brahmin who begged from a king. The king intended to go out hunting and ordered the brahmin to stay in the palace hall, saying, "Wait for me; I shall return."
He then went out on a hunt to pursue wild animals and became separated from his ministers; arriving in the midst of a mountain valley, he encountered a ghost who wished to devour him.
The King said, "Listen to my words."
This morning, while at the city gate, I encountered a practitioner begging from me. I said to him, "Stop;
wait for me on the palace terrace.
Now, please allow me to return briefly so that I may give this to the practitioner; I shall then come back to you to receive your meal.
The ghost said, "I now wish to devour you; would you truly be willing to come back?
The king replied:
"How excellent! Truly, for one who has no faith, shall I now take heed of this practitioner?
The ghost then released the king; the king returned to his palace, brought forth goods to give to the practitioner, entrusted the kingdom to the crown prince, and returned once more to the ghost.
When the ghost saw the King arrive, it was moved by his utmost sincerity; it offered its respects and thanked him, not daring to eat.
The Master said, "If the King can preserve his life and save his kingdom through such single-minded sincerity, how much more so should a worthy person uphold the Five Precepts?"
"If one gives with a sincere heart, the merit thereof is immeasurable.
(41) Once, King Aśoka was fond of giving alms-food to śramaṇas and ordered his crown prince to personally prepare the offerings. The prince, harboring silent resentment, said:
"When I become king, I shall kill all these practitioners of the Way."
The man of the Way, knowing in his heart that the Prince was filled with resentment, said to him:
"I shall not remain long in this world.
The Prince asked in alarm:
"The practitioner's insight is so profound that he knows my thoughts.
He then reflected:
"When I become king, I shall provide for this practitioner with offerings even greater than those given by my father."
When his mind became harmonious, he abandoned evil and turned toward the good.
The practitioner said,
"By the time you had become king, I had already been reborn in the heavens."
The Prince said, "How holy is this śramaṇa! Later, when he became king,
he made the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions the basis of his governance, whereby the realm eventually attained great prosperity and peace.

42. (Forty-two) Once, there was a man of the four castes who took two wives. The elder wife daily provided excellent food for a śramaṇa; the śramaṇa went every day to receive the food, which vexed the younger wife to the point of resentment.
The next day, when the śramaṇa came again, the young wife went out to take his bowl, placed impure matter inside it, put rice on top, and returned it to the śramaṇa.
The śramaṇa took it away; when he was about to eat in the mountains, he saw that it was impure and washed his bowl, after which he did not dare go there again.

The mouth and body of the young woman were both foul-smelling, so everyone who saw her fled and avoided her. Later, at the end of her life, she fell into the Hell of Boiling Excrement. Thus she transmigrated through the three evil realms for tens of millions of years. When her retribution was exhausted and she obtained human form, she constantly craved to eat excrement but could not, suffering from agonizing pain in her belly.
Later, when she became a wife, she would rise at night to steal and eat excrement.
She did this repeatedly until her husband, finding it strange, went to investigate and saw his wife eating feces.
This is the result of actions performed in previous lives.
There are four things difficult for a person to accomplish:

first, the construction of a stupa; second, the building of a monastery for the *saṃgha* of the four quarters; third, providing food to the community of bhikṣus; and fourth, leaving the household life to become a śramaṇa.
When these four matters are established, the merit is immeasurable.
Why is this? Because such things occur only occasionally within the three realms.

Having already attained human status and possessing wealth and property, one is further able to uproot the root of stinginess and greed, bestowing gifts and benefits at the appropriate time; that such a person establishes their meritorious deeds purely is likewise difficult to find.
"Who can know this merit?
Only the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Monks do not become kin through the mutual exchange of food and drink; rather, they become kin only through the mutual instruction and admonition of the sutras and the Dharma.

When monks mutually offer and bestow delicious food and delicacies upon one another, they gain a good reputation among monks in this world, but in the next world they will have no standing, and they will incur ill repute before the Buddha."
Why is this? Those who follow external paths see a bhikṣu and say:
"The disciples of the Buddha merely eat fine rice and give good clothing to one another; who taught them this?"
"This is the Buddha. Thus they harbor ill-will toward the Buddha.
It is only through the mutual invitation of monks by means of the sūtras, precepts, and the Way of the Dharma that they become truly close and intimate friends.
Why is this? Those who follow external paths and hold views of practice say to the bhikṣus:
"The disciples of the Buddha merely transmit the teachings, precepts, and path-dharma to one another; there is nothing else given."
"In this present life, a bhikṣu gains a good reputation, and in future lives, he attains liberation; thus, he has a virtuous discourse regarding the Buddha. Why is this so?

The Buddha is the teacher of the bhikṣus, and he instructs his disciples solely through the Way of the Sūtras. For this reason, it is not necessary to offer food as a gift; rather, one simply bestows upon one another the gift of virtuous words."
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should practice contentment. What is meant by practicing contentment?

It means seeking only one robe and one meal, always remaining mindful while walking in meditation (caṅkrama), not thinking of seeking elsewhere, and being able to restrain oneself so that the mind is not distracted; this is called contentment."

Furthermore, one should not consider oneself satisfied with what is called the sutras and precepts, nor with the attainment of the four dhyānas and the four formless concentrations, nor even with the stages of srotāpanna or sakṛdāgāmin; these are not yet grounds for considering oneself satisfied.
"In this way, it is sufficient not to calculate [the faults].
(43) There was a bhikṣu who, while on his alms-round, stopped on the road in a cramped place and suddenly urinated. Seeing him, the passers-by all mocked him together, saying:
"The disciples of the Buddha have a proper method in their gait and maintain dignity in their attire; yet this bhikṣu stands still and urinates—this is truly laughable!"
At that time, there was a wandering ascetic of the Nirgrantha clan who, seeing people mocking this bhikṣu, thought to himself:
"We Nirgranthas wander about naked, yet no one questions us;
but the disciples of the Buddha stand urinating, and everyone mocks them."
"In this way, our teachers lack a fixed system of rules; therefore, people do not laugh at them.
It is only because the Dharma of the Buddha’s disciples is pure, possesses ritual propriety, and is easy to discuss."
He then took refuge in the Buddha and became a śramaṇa, immediately attaining the stage of srotāpanna.

Bhikṣus, you are like lions, the kings among all beasts; as teachers among men, you must employ the Dharma in your speech. In your walking, standing, sitting, and rising, you must maintain dignified deportment. As models for humanity, you must not disparage yourselves; to disparage and ruin yourselves is to bring shame upon the sages of old.
Śakra, the King of Devas, together with the four Great Kings, surveys the world three times on the fifteenth day to see who maintains the precepts;
upon seeing those who maintain the precepts, the devas rejoice.
At that time, on the fifteenth day, Śakra, King of Devas, while seated upon his throne in the main hall, thought to himself:
"If those in the world observe the three fasts on the fifteenth day, they shall attain my rank when their lives end."
The devas at the periphery were greatly alarmed and said,
"Only by observing the three fasts on the fifteenth day can one attain a state such as that of Śakra.
A bhikṣu who had already attained arhatship, knowing immediately Śakra’s thoughts, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Can you truly verify whether what Śakra said was so?
The Buddha said, “Śakra’s words are not to be trusted; he spoke them without truth.”
Why is this? One who practices the three fasts with diligence on the fifteenth day may attain transcendence from the world; why then remain in the realm of Śākya?
To speak thus is not a truthful statement and is not worthy of belief.
"Who is able to know the merit of this fast? Only the Buddha.
(44) In the ocean there was a great dragon who wished to send rain upon Jambudvīpa, yet he feared that the earth would not be able to sustain such water.
The dragon thought to himself:
"There is no one on earth who can withstand my rain; I shall simply rain back into the sea.

Likewise, the disciples of the Buddha possess such great majesty and virtue that if they were to bestow their gifts upon the ninety-six kinds of external practitioners, there would likely be none capable of enduring them. Therefore, the disciples of the Buddha merely give to one another in succession, just as the dragon rains back into the sea from which he came.

45. Once there was a brahmin one hundred and twenty years of age who had never married since his youth and harbored no lustful desires. He dwelt in a desolate mountain wilderness, making a hut of *māo* grass and using thistles and weeds for a mat; he took fruits and melons for his food and did not accumulate wealth or treasures.
The king sought to marry her, but she would not go, intending instead to dwell in tranquility and non-action.
For several thousand years in the mountains, she took pleasure daily with various birds and beasts; there were four animals:
first, a fox; second, a monkey; third, an otter; and fourth, a hare.

These four beasts would daily listen to the monk’s recitation of the sūtras and the exposition of the precepts. As time passed in this manner, the various fruits and melons they ate were completely exhausted.
Later, when the monk intended for them to depart, these four beasts became deeply distressed and unhappy, and they deliberated together, saying:
"Let us each go out to seek and provide offerings for the monk."
The monkey went to another mountain and returned with sweet fruit to offer to the practitioner, saying, "I pray you do not depart.

The fox likewise transformed itself into a human being and, having obtained a bag of rice and flour for food, brought it to the practitioner; it was enough to provide a month's provisions, and he requested him to remain.
The otter also entered the water again and brought back a large fish to give to the practitioner, providing him with a month’s worth of provisions and saying, "I pray that you will not depart.
The hare thought to himself,
"What should I use to make an offering to the practitioner?"
He thought to himself,
"I should offer my own body as an offering.
He then went out to gather firewood to kindle a fire and produce charcoal, and went to inform the practitioner, saying:
"Now I am the smallest and most insignificant of rabbits; I can invite you into the fire to roast, using my body to provide for the Wayfarer’s needs for one day's provisions.
The rabbit then threw itself into the fire, yet the fire would not burn.
The practitioner saw the rabbit and, moved by its benevolence and righteousness, felt such deep compassion for it that he stopped and remained behind.
The Buddha said:
"The Brahmin at that time was the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; the rabbit was my own self; the monkey was Śāriputra; the fox was Ānanda; and the otter was Maudgalyāyana."

46 (46). Once, five practitioners of the Way were traveling together when they encountered snow and rain on the road. They passed by a shrine temple and stayed there for the night; inside the hall was a divine image that was worshipped by the officials and common people of the country.
The four men said, "It is bitterly cold tonight; we may take this wooden man and burn it for cooking. One man said:
"This is something used by humans; it must not be destroyed.
Thus, they left it unbroken.
A ghost within this room was constantly devouring people, and they spoke among themselves, saying:
"Right now, while we are eating that one person, he alone fears me, whereas the other four are wicked and must not be offended.
As for those who had desisted and dared not break the statue, they heard the ghosts speaking at night;
they rose and called their companions, saying, "Why do you not take this statue and break it to use for cooking?"
He then took it and burned it; when the human-demon (piśāca) smelled it, he fled in haste.
When one practices the Way, one must always maintain a firm mind; one must not be timid or weak, allowing demons and spirits to find an opportunity against oneself.

47 (Forty-seven): Once there was a king who abandoned his kingdom to become a śramaṇa. He practiced intensive meditation in the mountains, making a hut of grass and weeds and a mat of thistles and brambles; thinking he had attained his goal, he laughed loudly, saying, "How delightful!"
A man from the borderlands asked him, "You seem happy;
now that you sit alone in the mountains studying the Way, what joy can there possibly be?
The śramaṇa replied:

"When I was a king, my anxieties were many: I feared that a neighboring king might seize my kingdom; I feared that people might plunder my wealth and property; I feared that I might be coveted for my riches by others; and I was constantly afraid that my ministers, greedy for my treasures, would turn against me at any moment."
"Now that I have become a śramaṇa, no one covets my interests; this joy is beyond words, and for this reason I say it is joyful.

(48) Once there was a king who greatly cherished the Way and its virtue. He would constantly circumambulate a stūpa, and before he had completed even a hundred circuits, a neighboring king arrived to attack and seize his kingdom. The attending ministers were struck with great terror and immediately went to inform the king, saying:
"An army has arrived."
"Only by leaving this revolving stupa, Great King, can you employ a strategic measure to repel the heavy host of invaders.
The king said, "I will allow the troops to come; I shall certainly not stop them."
His mind remained as it was, and before he had finished circumambulating the stupa, the soldiers dispersed and departed.
A person who possesses single-minded concentration can eliminate anything whatsoever.

49 (49) Once there was a king who, when passing by the Buddha on his regular rounds, would pay him homage without avoiding mud or rain. His attendants were distressed by this and spoke among themselves:
The King asked, "Why is Your Majesty so preoccupied with such trivial matters?
When the King heard this, he returned to the palace and commanded his ministers:
"Go and seek out the heads of a hundred animals, as well as one human head, and bring them here."
The ministers addressed the king, saying:
"We have carried out Your Majesty’s command and sold [the other items] in the marketplace, and they were all sold; however, the human head could not be sold.
The ministers further reported this.
"The heads of the hundred beasts were all sold, yet this human head is foul and putrid; from the start, there has been no buyer.
The King said to his attendants, "It is simply that you do not understand."
"Bi, previously when you went to where the Buddha was and paid him homage, you people said, 'The King's mind is fragmented and distracted.

If you wish to know what my head is like—it is such that the head of a dead man is impure; one should seek merit so as to attain rebirth in heaven—and yet you, being foolish and ignorant, instead say it is 'fragmented'?"
The attendant minister said,
"It is indeed as the Great King has stated.
He bowed his head to apologize for his transgression:
"We, your subjects, are foolish and lack understanding.
Later, when the king went out again, all the ministers dismounted from their horses and paid homage to the Buddha, regarding the King as the Dharma.
(50) Once, there was a king who went on a tour; whenever he saw a śramaṇa, he would immediately alight from his carriage and pay homage to the śramaṇa. A practitioner said:
"Great King, stop; you must not descend from your carriage.
The King said, "I am ascending, not descending."

As for why it is said that one goes upward and does not go downward: now, when I pay homage to those who follow the Way, after my life comes to an end, I shall be reborn in the heavens; therefore, I say "upward" and not "downward."
51 (51). Once, after a person had died, his spirit returned and was rubbing its own old bones.
A bystander asked him, "You are already dead; why do you continue to rub these withered bones?"
The spirit said: "This was my former body.

It did not kill living beings, did not steal, did not commit adultery, nor did it engage in double-tongued speech, harsh abuse, lying, or frivolous talk; it was without envy, without malice, and without delusion. After death, it attained rebirth in the heavens, where its wishes were spontaneously fulfilled and its happiness was boundless. For this reason, I cherish and value it."
52. Once, in a foreign land, there was a śramaṇa practicing the Way in the mountains. A ghost manifested through transformation as a headless man and came before the śramaṇa, saying:

"There is no suffering from headaches. The eyes exist for seeing forms; the ears for hearing sounds; the nose for perceiving fragrances; and the mouth for receiving flavors. To be entirely without a head—how joyful that is!"
The ghost vanished again and reappeared transformed, having no body but possessing only hands and feet. The śramaṇa said:
"One who has no body does not know pain or itching; lacking the five viscera, one is entirely unaware of illness—how truly blissful!"
The ghost vanished again and reappeared as a man without hands or feet, who approached the śramaṇa from one side of the chariot wheel. The practitioner said:
"How wonderful!"
"Having no hands or feet, I am unable to go and seize the wealth of others; how joyful this is!
The ghost said, "The śramaṇa maintains one-pointedness of mind and remains unmoving."

The ghost then transformed himself into a handsome man and came before the practitioner, bowing his head at the practitioner’s feet and saying, “The practitioner’s resolve is so firm; what you are now studying will surely be accomplished before long.”
He bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet in reverence and departed.
(53) Once, while a śramaṇa was practicing the Way in the mountains, his inner robe slipped off onto the ground; he looked around to left and right, then slowly pulled the robe back up and put it on.
A mountain deity emerged and said to the practitioner, "There are no people here at all;
why do you crawl on the ground to pick up your robe when it has fallen?
The śramaṇa replied:
"The mountain deities see me, and I likewise see them; the sun, moon, and the various devas above also see me. Is it not unreasonable for my body to be thus exposed?
To have no sense of shame or remorse is to be no disciple of the Buddha."
54 (54). Once there were six people who traveled as companions; they all fell together into hell and were placed in the same cauldron, where each wished to recount his own past transgressions.
One person says "sha," two people say "na," three people say "te," four people say "she," five people say "gu," and six people say "tuo-luo."
The Buddha saw this and smiled. Maudgalyāyana asked the Buddha, "For what reason do you smile?
The Buddha said:

"There were six people who, as companions, together fell into hell; they were all in a single cauldron, each wishing to recount their original transgressions, but as the boiling water surged and splashed, they could not speak more than once, for as soon as each uttered a single word, they were driven down."
The first person said, "As for 'sha' (sa), sixty billion years in this world constitutes a single day in the hells; when will it ever end?
The second person said, "As for 'na' (na), there is no fixed limit, nor does one know when one shall attain liberation."
The third person said, "What is this 'special' about? Alas! Why must you pursue a livelihood in such a manner?

Being unable to restrain your own mind, you have seized the share belonging to the five families to provide for the Triple Gem; yet you remain foolishly greedy and insatiable—what benefit is there now in regret?"
The fourth person spoke of the "involved," saying that even his livelihood was not sincere; he thought, "My property belongs to others, and I may suffer pain on their account.

The fifth person spoke of the "temporary," asking, "Who can guarantee that I shall emerge from hell and no longer violate the prohibitions of the Path, thereby attaining birth among gods and humans in bliss?"

The sixth person says: "As for 'Dhara' (the burden), this matter was not originally intended by my mind. It is like a charioteer who loses the path and enters a wrong road; when the axle breaks, there is no time for regret."

55 (55) *Seven Excerpts of Parables on Arhats*, Part 7: Formerly, the Buddha dispatched Śāriputra to travel west to the world-system of Veṣṭhila-vyūha to inquire after that Buddha regarding three matters:
“Is the Buddha’s person at ease and secure?”... [and so forth].
"Is the Dharma being taught as usual?
Are those who receive it making progress?
Śāriputra, immediately receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, went to that land and proclaimed these words.
That Buddha replied, "All are perfectly secure.

At that time, that Buddha turned the wheel of *avaivartika* and preached the Dharma for Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage. Having heard this, Śāriputra returned from that land; his countenance, radiance, and gait were more excellent than usual.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"When you arrived there, for what reason were you walking with such a composed and joyful air?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Suppose, for example, a person who is poor, hungry, and cold were to obtain a great treasure as vast as Mount Sumeru;
would they not be filled with joy? The Buddha said, “Excellent!”

Śāriputra said: "When I arrived at that land, I was able to hear that Buddha expound upon the profound matters of *avaivartika* [non-retrogression]; for this reason, I am filled with such exultation that I cannot contain myself."
The Buddha said: "Excellent! It is as you have said."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“Suppose there were a great householder, a mahākāravaṭa, who possessed only purple-gold and maṇi-jewels as his treasures. Inside [his house], there was a copper, iron, lead, or tin vessel that had been discarded outside among the refuse. A person in poverty and destitution, finding it, joyfully took it back home, saying, ‘I have obtained a great treasure of the mahākāravaṭa! Would that [vessel] truly be a rare and wonderful treasure of the householder?”
He replied, "No. The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"What you have heard and attained is merely for such as the poor; what that Buddha taught concerns only the matters of the ten stages and those who are pure within the exhortations. What you have heard is not even worth mentioning."
Śāriputra was immediately stricken with grief and distress, as if saying, "I thought I had obtained treasure, yet it turns out to be lead and tin.

When Śāriputra spoke these words, countless people all gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, equal enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and countless people attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
56 (56). Formerly, Mahāmaudgalyāyana sat beneath a tree to test his own vision of the Path; seeing eight thousand Buddha-fields, he thought to himself:
"Even what the Tathāgata sees is not superior to mine."
He walked with the gait of a lion toward the place where the Buddha was.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana,
“You who belong to the lineage of the śrāvakas, why do you now walk with the gait of a lion?”
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:

“As for what I myself have seen in the eight directions across eight thousand buddha-fields, I believe that what the Buddha perceives is far beyond my own vision; therefore, he walks with the lion’s stride.”
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, Maudgalyāyana!
Your vision is as vast and great as this."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“For example, it is like comparing the light of a lamp to a maṇi jewel; the difference between them is immense.
The Buddha said:

"With my eyes, I see as many lands in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges Rivers; taking each grain of sand to represent a single Buddha-land, I see everything contained within them all."

There are those who come from Tuṣita Heaven to enter their mothers’ wombs, as well as those who are born, those who leave home to practice the Way, those who subdue Māra, those for whom Śakra and Brahmā come to offer encouragement and assistance, those who turn the wheel of Dharma and preach all teachings, those who wish to enter parinirvāṇa, and those who have already entered parinirvāṇa and had their śarīras cremated; such as these are beyond counting, and with this eye I have seen them all.

The Buddha emitted light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which shone through to the upper realms; he emitted light from within his body, which illuminated the eight directions; and he emitted light from beneath his feet, which clearly illumined the lower realms, each extending across hundreds of thousands of *kṣetras*. At that moment, the lands of the ten directions shook in six ways, and that great radiance was unimpeded by anything.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana, right before the Buddha, beheld countless thousands of Ganges-sands of boundless lands; everything within them was as previously described by the Buddha. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the ten Ganges-sands of lands mentioned by the Buddha just now, are those the very ones now manifested by the Buddha?"
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana, “It was only because of your lack of faith that I spoke in brief; what I have now manifested is beyond measure.
Upon hearing these words, Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately collapsed to the ground like a great mountain falling, and wailed aloud with a loud cry:

"I recall that the Buddha possesses such merits; even now he is like this. Would it not be better for my own body to enter the great niraya than for me to see him lying on his right side for more than a hundred kalpas without attaining arhatship?"
Maudgalyāyana then said:

"As for those present in this assembly, even though the World-Honored One has declared me foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), I am not even worthy of mention; my accumulated merit does not equal even a fraction of knowing this, let alone those who have attained nothing at all."
"Those who have resolved their minds should aspire to be like the Buddha; do not emulate me by becoming seeds that fail to sprout.

Among the countless thousands of dragons, spirits, and people gathered there, all gave rise to the supreme and impartial intention for universal deliverance. Those who resolved their minds upon the Great Way immediately attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), and those who had already attained non-retrogression all reached the dwelling of *avaivartika*.

57 (Fifty-seven): In the past, there was a dragon king named Badi, whose majestic spiritual power was vast and far-reaching, moving many to awe. His disposition was impetuous and irritable, and he frequently acted with violence and cruelty. He often conspired with other dragons to bring about unlawful winds, rains, and thunderbolts; hailstorms killed countless people, birds, beasts, and crawling insects.
There were ten thousand venerable arhats who deliberated among themselves, saying:
"If one kills a single person, one falls into hell for one kalpa; even after a hundred such deaths as retribution for the crime, the debt would still not be fully paid."

Now this dragon has been inflicting harm upon living beings in incalculable numbers from beginning to end; as he shows no sign of ceasing, we fear he will be difficult to save. It would be fortunate indeed if we were to go together to admonish him and stop him.
At that time, the Buddha, knowing this, praised them, saying: "Excellent!

You have left the household life to seek the path of the unconditioned (*asamskṛta*), desiring to rescue all lives in peril and distress and to deliver those who have committed offenses. This is truly most wonderful; such is the way to repay your debt of gratitude."
At that time, the arhats said to one another, "It is not fitting that ten thousand people should go together.
Thereupon, each of them went separately, but they were immediately beset by calamities and could not advance; returning, they said to one another:

"Although I traveled alone, I was unable to subdue, transform, or humble this dragon and cause him to change for the better; I must now gather the merit of ten thousand people and travel together with them all. Thus, they set out once again.

The dragon unleashed wind, rain, thunder, hail, and lightning; ten thousand people were struck with terror, not knowing where it had come from, and having been humiliated by its defiance, they prostrated themselves and returned.

Ānanda said to the Buddha: “This dragon has slaughtered as many as these people and various beasts; its transgressions are so great that they cannot be calculated. Now, moreover, it has added the terror of hail to ten thousand arhats, raining down upon their robes like one drowning; its sins are profound and vast, beyond further reckoning.”

At that time, the Buddha was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa together with ten thousand bodhisattvas and ten thousand arhats. He traveled to another mountain, arriving at the dwelling place of a nāga. The nāga then became enraged and raised a violent storm of rain, thunder, hail, and lightning; he discharged a single hailstone capable of covering an area of forty zhang square, which, upon hitting the ground, would sink four chi deep, intending thereby to harm the Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattvas.

At that time, as the hail was falling, it stayed suspended in mid-air and transformed into celestial flowers. The Buddha emitted a brilliant light that illuminated everything extensively; the more than ten thousand people who were hunting in the mountains encountered the dark clouds and rain, becoming disoriented and unable to distinguish east from west, yet they all followed the light to the place where the Buddha resided.

The dragon struck again with a thunderclap, releasing a boulder forty *zhang* square; had the stone reached the ground, it would have sunk forty *zhang* deep into the earth. Instead, above the Buddha, it merged with the previous flowers to transform into a floral canopy. The small dragon likewise released hailstones, each one *zhang* square, which all behaved in the same manner.

When the Arhats previously saw the calamity brought by the dragon, each felt terror and drew near to take refuge with the Buddha. From within the clouds, the dragon saw that the hailstones had transformed into flower-canopies suspended in the void without descending. He then thought to himself:
"I shall coil my body firmly into a shape forty *zhang* in length, intending to hurl it upon the Buddha and the assembly of monks."

Immediately, he threw himself down, but could not strike a vital spot; his entire body was racked with pain, and he lay prostrate on the ground for a very long time. Raising his head and opening his eyes, he looked up and saw the Buddha, thinking, "Everything I have done has failed as intended; I suspect this must be a venerable, wondrous, and unsurpassed divine being."

Thereupon, the young dragons all threw themselves down, yet remained unmoved; at that moment, the Dragon King’s life ended and he was reborn as a deva, while the other young dragons likewise all died together and became sons of devas, all of whom came down and stood by the Buddha’s side.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Do you know from where this deva has come? He replied:

“It was not so,” the Buddha said. “Regarding those dragons who previously gave rise to evil intentions, you said their offenses were great and beyond measure; yet they threw themselves to the ground and conceived a single thought of goodness, recognizing the Buddha as supreme. Because their lives ended with this state of mind, they have been reborn as devas. This is precisely what it means.”
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the devas and all the sons of heaven conceived the aspiration for supreme, impartial liberation.
At that time, the hunters who had come from the mountains to visit the Buddha each thought to themselves:
"If even this dragon’s transgressions can lead to liberation, then the harm I have done is surely no more than a trifle compared to his."
As he wished to give rise to the aspiration for the Way, his mind remained hesitant.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"These ten thousand arhats wish to deliver these sinners, yet their power is insufficient for the task. If I were not present, they would be restrained by the nāgas; they would be unable to deliver the evil ones and would instead cause their transgressions to increase."

If you wish to deliver all beings, you must first enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and contemplate those who can be delivered; only then should you act. As for those whom you cannot deliver, whether the Tathāgata delivers them or not is his prerogative.
At that time, having heard these words, all the hunters conceived the aspiration for supreme, impartial liberation.
As for the devas, nāgas, and humans present in the assembly, the Buddha preached the sūtra for them, and they all attained the stage of *avaivartika*.

In the past, the Dragon King Badi and Śākyamuni Buddha were both brahmins. At that time, Badi had ten thousand disciples; when they saw that Śākyamuni was a man of exceptional talent, they abandoned their teacher to serve Śākyamuni. Badi harbored resentment for this, and as a result of his transgression, he became a dragon.

The Buddha’s virtues having been perfected, he had already delivered many beings; his ten thousand disciples had all attained arhatship. Consequently, the malevolence of the dragon grew rampant as it sought to inflict widespread harm. Out of compassion for these ten thousand people, the Buddha desired to go and deliver them.

Because he had previously been his teacher, although the four paths were complete, he still suffered humiliation from him; had he been a Bodhisattva, even if a dragon wished to inflict harm, he would never have dared.

(58) Once there was a country where the population was flourishing, yet the men and women, both old and young, committed all manner of evils; their natures were stubborn, perverse, and violent, making them difficult to transform.

The Buddha took his disciples to a neighboring kingdom. The five hundred arhats felt conceited in their hearts, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana came forward and said to the Buddha, "I wish to go there to deliver the people."
The Buddha immediately granted his permission.
[The man] went to preach the Way of the Sūtras, saying, "One should do good; if one commits various evils, the retribution for such sins is unfathomable.
However, the entire population of the country covered him in abuse and beat him, refusing to follow his teachings. Thereupon, he returned once more.
Śāriputra said to Maudgalyāyana:
“If you wish to instruct these people, you should do so with wisdom, lest they again meet with disparagement.
Śāriputra then addressed the Buddha:
"I wish to go there to exhort and deliver the people.
The Buddha again granted him permission to go.
He preached the sutras and the precepts for them, but they did not follow his instructions and instead insulted him by spitting upon him.

Mahākāśyapa and his honored disciples, numbering five hundred in all, went there one after another in succession; yet they were unable to convert them and were all treated with contempt and insult. Ānanda said to the Buddha:

“The people of that country are wicked and do not accept wholesome teachings, inflicting many humiliations. The sin of insulting a single arhat is immeasurable; how much more so for defying the instructions of so many people? They shall incur a grave retribution that even empty space cannot contain.”
The Buddha said:
"Although this offense is profound and heavy, the Bodhisattva regards it as tranquil and without fault.
The Buddha then dispatched Mañjuśrī to go and deliver him.
Upon arriving in that country, they all praised him, saying:
"How joyful is what the worthy one has accomplished!

They went before the king and extolled him face-to-face, ensuring that everyone, high and low, heard and knew of it, saying: "So-and-so is brave and strong; so-and-so is again benevolent and filial; so-and-so possesses courage and wisdom. Wherever he was, they praised him according to their inclinations, and everyone rejoiced beyond measure, saying:
"This Great Being’s teaching is sublime; he knows my aspirations—how wonderful and auspicious!

Each person took gold, jewels, incense, and flowers, scattering them over the Bodhisattva. They all presented fine silks, brocades, garments, and delicacies of sweet and savory flavors as offerings to the Bodhisattva, and all resolved to attain the supreme, impartial mind of universal liberation.
Mañjuśrī said to the people:
"Your making offerings to me is not as good as giving them to my teacher. My teacher is named Buddha; you should go together to offer to him, for the merit will be immeasurably doubled."

Everyone was greatly delighted and followed Mañjuśrī to the place where the Buddha was. The Buddha preached the sūtra for them, and they immediately attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) at that very moment. The three thousandfold world system shook violently, and the mountains, forests, and trees all uttered these words of praise:
"Mañjuśrī has skillfully delivered such beings."
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Where now are these deep and great sins?
Five hundred arhats fell to the ground and wept.
“If such is the transformation wrought by the majestic spiritual power of a bodhisattva, how much more so for a Tathāgata?
I am a ruined seed, of no benefit to anyone.”

59 (59). Once, when the Buddha was sitting beneath a tree, he preached the Dharma for countless people. Among them, some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, some *sakṛdāgāmin*, some *anāgāmin*, and some attained the state of *arhat*; such as these were beyond counting.
At that time, the Buddha’s face lacked its usual radiant luster and appeared as if he were sorrowful. Ānanda, deeply perceiving the Buddha’s intention, knelt for a long time and addressed the Buddha:
"I have attended upon the Buddha with reverence for eight years, yet I have never before seen the Honored Countenance of the Buddha devoid of radiance as it is today."
What transformation could have occurred to cause the Buddha to act thus?
Today, who has failed in the Great Practice?
Who has committed evil and fallen into hell?
"Who is there that has departed far from the original limit?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Suppose, for example, a merchant carrying many precious treasures and several tens of millions of coins travels a great distance in search of profit, but on the way encounters bandits and loses his wealth. He remains naked, with no means to sustain himself; would he not be filled with sorrow and anxiety?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“His grief is most intense.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Since countless kalpas past, I have practiced the Way with diligent toil, desiring to rescue and deliver all people so that they might all attain Buddhahood. Now that I have attained Buddhahood for myself, yet there is not a single person who has performed meritorious deeds, I am therefore displeased that the color of my body has changed."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:

“Now, among the disciples of the Buddha, those who have attained arhatship—whether they have passed away, are currently living, or will yet come—cannot be counted. Those who have attained the stage of anāgāmin, sakṛdāgāmin, and srotāpanna are likewise beyond calculation. How then can there be one who crosses over by means of merit without a cause?”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Suppose an old man and an old woman have ten or more daughters; would they be able to manage the household and sustain the family lineage? Ānanda replied:
"It is not possible," the Buddha said.
"Though there may be countless thousands of Arhats who have been born through my Dharma, they are still not my sons; for even they would ultimately be unable to sit beneath the Bodhi tree."
"It is as if there are many daughters born into a family, yet when they are married off, only the father, mother, and grandmother are left alone;

I am just like this. At that time, the Buddha wept and shed three drops of tears, and the trichiliocosm shook violently. Innumerable devas, nāgas, spirits, and humans all conceived the aspiration for supreme, equal liberation. Instantly, the Buddha’s countenance became upright, handsome, and serene; countless rays of light underwent thousands of billions of transformations, illuminating the ten directions with a brilliance twice that of usual times. Those who beheld these lights were all saved and delivered.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"Why is the divine transformation of the repeated radiance so wondrous and excellent?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"It is like an old man or woman who worships heaven and prays to the earth for offspring; when they finally obtain a son and he is able to establish the family lineage, would they not be filled with joy and congratulate themselves?"
"Now all those who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna are filled with joy, for the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed.

The Buddha dispatched the Bodhisattva Sumati to sixty billion *koṭis* of lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, commanding him to go to those realms and fetch lion thrones, various foods, and utensils for drink. He returned here in the time it takes to extend one's arm; having adorned and prepared the high and vast lion thrones, he invited all beings without exception. Those who had resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of universal liberation all sat upon natural lion thrones atop thousand-petaled golden lotuses.

Some sat within pavilions draped with canopies of the seven treasures or beneath trees made of the seven treasures; they erected various banners and streamers with handles made of the seven treasures, while the banners were of celestial brocade and the flowered parasols were of heavenly silk.
The Buddha, at that moment, caused the great trichiliocosm to transform into bathing pools, filled with seven-jeweled lotuses that sprang up therein.

The Buddha himself transformed his body to appear as a bodhisattva, or again manifested forms like those of Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Heavenly Kings, extensively providing great almsgiving to all. The fragrance of the food of ten thousand flavors was widely perceived throughout the ten directions; all who smelled the fragrance of the food conceived the aspiration for supreme, impartial liberation. As the fragrance permeated their bodies and issued forth from their pores, those who in turn smelled the fragrance from the pores likewise conceived the aspiration for supreme, impartial liberation.

The boundless lands of the ten directions shook with great trembling, and from every land, the Buddhas each dispatched their foremost attendant Bodhisattvas to offer congratulations; this was because Śākyamuni had employed all means, and many among the people had resolved to attain the mind of a Bodhisattva.

Among them, some came bringing purple-gold lotuses, some came bringing mani-jewel lotuses, and some brought moon-bright pearl lotuses; each carried various precious jewel lotuses and together scattered them over the Buddha.

By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, all the scattered flowers were transformed into a single flower-canopy that covered and pervaded countless lands throughout the ten directions. The radiance of this flower-canopy also illuminated those lands, providing constant light to places of darkness. Those in the hells (*niraya*), the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), and among birds, beasts, and domestic animals all conceived the Great Resolve and desired to seek Buddhahood. For the sake of the entire assembly, the Buddha preached the sutra; incalculable bodhisattvas attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), further incalculable devas and humans attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena), further incalculable nāgas, spirits, and people attained the state of *avaivartika*, and all the bodhisattvas and *saṃsārin* beings conceived the resolve for supreme, equal liberation.

60. Once there was a man who, being young and impoverished, traveled to another country and obtained a sweet fruit. It was fragrant, delicious, and large—rare in the world—and he cherished it so much that he did not dare to eat it. Thinking of his parents and wishing to give the fruit to them, he immediately took it and returned to Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Buddha entered the city together with the bodhisattvas and great disciples, proceeding to the house of the elder to accept the host’s invitation.
Just as the Buddha had departed and before the others had reached the house, she took the fruit in her hand and cast it toward the place where the Buddha was.

From my youth until my maturity, I had never heard of a Buddha nor seen the footprints of a Buddha; yet now, seeing the wheel-marks like parasols, their radiance and manifold transformations complete and without deficiency, I stood by his feet and gazed at them without weariness, my heart filled with a sense of fortunate coincidence, free from both sorrow and joy.

"If even the tracks left by the earth are such as this, how much more so is this person—who is truly not of this world. This practitioner who has crossed over will surely return; I shall set aside my share for my parents and wait for this person to arrive so that I may offer it to them."
Before the Buddha had finished his circumambulation, the man sat beside the tracks, weeping with sorrowful reflection. A traveler passing along the road asked him:
"Are you sitting here grieving because you have lost your fruit?"

He replied, “I have been guarding these traces of the Infinite Honored One, awaiting the arrival of the divine personage in hopes that he would return. I wished to offer this fruit as my own humble dedication to him; however, I have long awaited his radiant countenance and have not yet fulfilled my wish. It is because I am so wretchedly lacking in merit that I grieve.”

Those who had been traveling and were questioning him gathered to watch like clouds; how could they not have thought this man was mad or deluded? How could they have known that the traveler was still there, and why would he wish to wait for him?

When the Buddha arrived at the house of the donor, the elder, he took his seat; once the assembly of monks had finished washing their hands and were seated in order, the elder, along with his sons and daughters, presented the rice and utensils, setting out all varieties of delicacies in full abundance.
The Buddha bestowed a blessing from afar; meanwhile, a person guarding the tracks along the road was holding fruit and stood with bated breath, desiring to approach the Buddha.
When the meal was finished, the donor thought to himself:
"I did not see the World-Honored One bestow a blessing upon me."
He then offered prayers from afar for those outside holding the fruit, wondering if what they were offering might be unacceptable.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The merit of the householder's offerings has already departed; though his preparations were extensive, his mind harbored expectations, and he held four fears while setting his will upon *nirvāṇa*."

Outside there was a youth who held sweet fruit in his hand with single-minded devotion and no other thought; he waited compassionately by my footprints, desiring to offer me the superior fruit, and for the sake of all beings, he resolved upon the Great Way.
"Therefore, let us all together offer alms from afar.
The elder thought to himself:
"This man indeed gives without any other food, yet the Buddha praises his virtue as being most sublime and wondrous."
"Although my wealth is great and my provisions are abundant, when weighed against the gravity of his merit, mine does not compare. I wish to attend upon the Buddha as he goes to see this man.
The Buddha then rose and proceeded to where the keeper of the tracks was; the Bodhisattva’s disciples, elders, householders, and the rest of the assembly followed him immediately.

Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, his physical marks and secondary characteristics surpassing the light of the sun and moon, the one who held the fruit went forward to meet him, prostrated himself in salutation, and then, kneeling with long-drawn knees, offered this fruit to the Buddha, immediately giving rise to the aspiration for supreme, universal liberation.

The Buddha emitted a radiance that illuminated infinitely, causing the trichiliocosm to tremble greatly; at that moment, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions all appeared, like reflections in a mirror, such that there was nothing—whether near or far—that was not seen.

The Buddha accepted their offerings and transferred them as gifts to all Buddhas and others, causing each single offering to pervade infinitely. From the *kāṣāya* robes of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions, they each extended hands of golden light and emitted thousands of billions of flames.

At the tip of each flame, there spontaneously appeared a precious lotus flower, a jeweled lattice canopy, and a lion throne; upon these sat Buddhas and various bodhisattvas, all of whom held precious alms bowls and received these fruits, each holding one fruit as they performed miraculous transformations and gave the *dakṣiṇā*.

Śākyamuni Buddha is likewise; he illuminates the ten directions from this world, filling all of space with divine beings and celestial deities. Throughout the eight cardinal and intermediate directions, above and below, there is no place left unoccupied, as all join in joy, praising and extolling him, so that all bodhisattvas throughout the three realms may receive his grace.
At that time, those of superior fruit attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the Buddha bestowed upon them this prediction:
"In the future, you shall become Buddhas, titled 'Fruition-Venerable King' (*Phala-guru-rāja*), Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened Ones; your lands shall be like the realm of Amitābha."
One should hear that in the distinct lands designated by the World-Honored One, beings naturally attain purity and the stage of *avaivartika*.
Countless elders and householders are directed toward the tracks of the Path; thousands have reached the stage of non-retrogression through great deliverance—such is the nature of their virtue.
61 (61). Once, the Buddha went to the second heaven of the Trāyastriṃśa gods to preach the Dharma for his mother.
At that time, there was a deva whose life span was nearing its end;

seven signs appeared as portents: first, the light from his neck vanished; second, the flowers adorning his head withered; third, his facial complexion changed; fourth, dust settled upon his robes; fifth, sweat broke out from beneath his armpits; sixth, his body became emaciated; and seventh, he departed from his original seat.
He then reflected to himself:

"After my life ends, I must abandon this celestial throne, the palace of the seven treasures, the bathing pools, the gardens and fruits, the spontaneous food and drink, and the music of the many celestial maidens; instead, I shall descend to be born as a child in the womb of a mangy sow in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī."
She was deeply filled with anxiety and sorrow, not knowing what expedient means she should employ to escape this transgression.
A deity spoke to her, saying:
"The Buddha is currently here preaching the sutra for his mother. The Buddha is the savior of all beings throughout the three periods of time; only the Buddha can deliver you from your sin."
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in homage, and before he had even had a chance to pose a question, the Buddha addressed the devaputra:
"All phenomena return to impermanence; this is something you have long known. Why, then, do you grieve?"
The deva addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Although I know that celestial blessings cannot be maintained for long, I regret that upon leaving this seat I shall become a piglet to a mange-ridden sow; yet, taking this as a bitter poison, I am merely accepting another body and do not dare to feel fear."
The Buddha said:

"If you wish to leave the body of a pig, you should take the Three Refuges, saying: 'Namo Buddha, Namo Dharma, Namo Bhikṣusaṃgha. Take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Bhikṣusaṃgha; do this three times each day."

The deva followed the Buddha’s teaching and took refuge day and night; seven days later, his life as a deva came to an end, and he descended to be born in the kingdom of Vaiśālī as the son of an elder. While in his mother’s womb, he took refuge three times daily, and upon being born and falling to the ground, he likewise knelt and took refuge.

When his mother gave birth, there was no postpartum discharge; the maidservant attending her became terrified and fled, and the mother also felt deep suspicion. When the child fell to the ground, he spoke, and she called him "Flux" (Yinghuo), intending to kill him.
She then reflected to herself: "My young son is strange; if I were to kill this child, my husband would surely hold me guilty."
"Tell the elder slowly; it will not be too late to kill him.
The mother immediately took her son and went to inform the elder, saying:

"I have given birth to a boy who, as soon as he fell to the ground, knelt down with palms joined and took refuge in the Triple Gem. The whole family was astonished by this and called him Yinghuo (the Planet Mars)."
The father said, "Stop, stop! This child is no ordinary being.

In a human life spent in this world for a hundred years, or perhaps eighty or ninety, one often does not even understand the need to take refuge in the Triple Gem; how much less could this child, upon falling to the ground, be able to recite 'Namo Buddha'?"
"Raise and care for him well; be careful not to treat him with negligence or contempt.

The boy subsequently grew up, and when he was nearly seven years old, he was playing with his peers by the side of the road. At that time, the disciples of the Buddha, Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, happened to pass by the boy's side. The boy came forward, prostrated at their feet, and said:
"I pay homage to Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were astonished that the child could pay homage to the bhikṣus.
The child said,
"Does the practitioner not recognize me?"
"The Buddha was preaching the sutras for his mother in the heavens; at that time, I was a pig dwelling below among the devas. Following the Buddha's teaching, I took refuge and attained human status.
The bhikṣu entered meditative concentration and immediately knew this, whereupon he offered a blessing, saying: "Cilika!"
The boy said to Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra:
"I pray that you use my voice to invite the World-Honored One, the assembly of Bodhisattvas, and yourselves."
Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra accepted his words accordingly. The boy then returned home and said to his parents:
"Just now, while playing, I saw two disciples of the Buddha passing by; I immediately invited the Buddha and the fourfold assembly for a meal, so please prepare some sweet and savory delicacies."

The parents loved him and followed his every word; they marveled at how, despite his youth, he had developed such great intelligence. Furthermore, they were struck by the excellence of his conduct and his knowledge of past lives, which were most precious and wondrous, surpassing all worldly fame and flavor. They sought to provide him with the finest and most exquisite things, exceeding even the boy's own expectations.
The Buddha and the assembly of monks, each by virtue of their own merit, manifested supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and arrived at the boy’s house for a meal.

After the parents and all others had completed the offerings, and the incense and water for washing were presented according to the Dharma, the Buddha preached the sutra for them. Thereupon, the parents, the son, and all their internal and external relatives attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) at that very moment.
If the merit of taking refuge is such as this, how much more so for one who practices the Way and its teachings throughout their entire life?
*The Old Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables*, Volume II.
